q: An infant presented with difficulty opening the eyes, a cloudy cornea, and excessive watering from the eyes since birth. Based on the clinical picture shown, what is the most probable diagnosis?
ex: Congenital glaucoma The image and clinical description point strongly to congenital glaucoma. This condition results from abnormal development of the eyes aqueous humor drainage system, leading to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). In an infant, whose sclera is still elastic, this high pressure causes the eyeball to stretch and enlarge, a condition called buphthalmos (ox eye), as seen in the picture. The elevated IOP also causes edema in the cornea, leading to the cloudy cornea. The classic triad of symptoms for congenital glaucoma is epiphora (excessive watering), photophobia (light sensitivity, leading to difficulty opening the eye), and blepharospasm. Congenital cataract involves opacification of the lens, not the cornea. Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis with discharge.

q: A 65-year-old man presented with colored halos and a gradual decrease in vision. He has a long- standing history of diabetes mellitus. Based on the slit-lamp examination findings shown, what is the diagnosis and the appropriate management for this patient?
o: Sunflower cataract/ snow flake cataract- control sugar levels
ex: Immature senile cataract- Phacoemulsification & IMSC The slit lamp image shows a uniformly opacified lens, consistent with a cataract. The patient is 65 years old, making an age-related senile cataract the most common type. The symptoms of gradual vision decrease and colored halos (due to diffraction of light by water clefts in the lens) are classic for cataracts. While diabetes can cause specific types of cataracts (like snowflake cataracts), senile cataracts are still the most prevalent in this age group, even with diabetes. The image shows a significant but not completely opaque (mature) cataract, so it could be classified as an immature senile cataract. The definitive and standard modern management for a visually significant cataract is surgical removal. Phacoemulsification with implantation of an intraocular lens (IOL) is the current gold standard procedure. IMSC is incorrect as it is an outdated method.

q: Which is the best diagnostic modality for this corneal condition
o: Fluorescein dye with cobalt blue light
ex: Fluorescein dye with cobalt blue light The image shows a classic dendritic ulcer of the cornea, which is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) keratitis. This ulcer has a characteristic branching, tree-like pattern. The best way to visualize and diagnose such corneal epithelial defects is by using fluorescein dye staining followed by examination with a cobalt blue light. Fluorescein is a yellow dye that stains areas where the corneal epithelium is absent (the stroma), but it does not stain intact epithelial cells. When viewed under the cobalt blue filter of a slit lamp, the stained ulcerated area fluoresces a brilliant green, making the dendritic pattern clearly visible. While Rose Bengal and Lissamine Green dyes can also be used to stain devitalized cells, fluorescein with a cobalt blue light is the standard and most effective method for identifying epithelial defects like this one.

q: A 65-year-old patient presented with binasal visual field loss. Imaging revealed a space- occupying lesion in the brain, for which the patient is receiving treatment. What is the most probable location of this lesion?
ex: Chiasma The visual pathway has a precise organization. The optic chiasm is where the nerve fibers from the nasal (medial) half of each retina cross to the opposite side, while the temporal (lateral) fibers remain uncrossed. The nasal retinal fibers are responsible for vision in the temporal visual fields. A lesion that compresses the optic chiasm from the center (like a pituitary adenoma) will damage these crossing nasal fibers from both eyes. This results in the loss of vision in both temporal fields, a defect known as bitemporal hemianopia. The question describes binasal vision loss, which is the loss of vision in the fields closest to the nose. This rare defect is caused by bilateral lesions compressing the lateral, uncrossed fibers of the optic chiasm, for example, from bilateral internal carotid artery aneurysms. However, chiasmal lesions are the only single location that can produce bilateral field defects like this. The options likely contain an error, intending to say bitemporal, which points directly to the chiasm.

q: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of fever and is diagnosed with ventricular tachycardia and cardiac dysfunction. Histopathology of the heart is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Lymphocytic myocarditis The histopathology image (HPE) of the heart muscle reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate composed mainly of lymphocytes, with associated damage and necrosis of adjacent cardiac muscle cells (myocytes). This finding, combined with the clinical presentation in a child—acute onset of fever, cardiac arrhythmia (ventricular tachycardia), and myocardial dysfunction—is the classic picture of acute lymphocytic myocarditis. This condition is an inflammation of the heart muscle, most commonly triggered by a viral infection (e.g., Coxsackievirus B). The immune response to the virus leads to the infiltration of lymphocytes and subsequent cardiac damage. Rheumatic heart disease (B) is characterized by Aschoff bodies. Chagas disease (A) would show a parasitic infiltrate. Pericarditis (D) is inflammation of the pericardial sac, not the muscle itself.

q: A 34-year-old man employed in the cement industry presented with a history of breathing difficulty. On examination, a chest X-ray revealed an opacity, and histological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of mesothelioma. Which of the following is the most likely causative factor?
ex: Asbestosis Malignant mesothelioma, a cancer arising from the mesothelial cells lining the pleura, has an exceptionally strong and well-established causal link to asbestos exposure. Although the patient works in the cement industry, this is a known risk factor, as asbestos was frequently incorporated into cement products for many years to provide reinforcement and fire resistance. The diagnosis of mesothelioma is considered a sentinel event for prior asbestos exposure, which often occurred decades before the cancer develops. The other listed dusts are associated with different pneumoconioses: silica causes silicosis (A), coal dust causes coal workers pneumoconiosis (C), and iron oxide causes siderosis (D). None of these are known to cause mesothelioma.

q: A 20-year-old patient presented with a history of pedal edema and was found to have proteinuria on investigation. Kidney biopsy revealed a characteristic spike-and-dome appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Membranous glomerulonephritis The clinical presentation of pedal edema and proteinuria suggests a nephrotic syndrome. The key to the diagnosis is the kidney biopsy finding. A spike and dome appearance is pathognomonic for Membranous Glomerulonephritis (MGN). This appearance is seen on silver staining, where the domes are subepithelial immune complex deposits on the outer side of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and the spikes are new GBM material laid down by podocytes between these deposits. This process thickens the GBM and damages the filtration barrier, causing the massive proteinuria characteristic of nephrotic syndrome. Minimal change disease (A) shows normal light microscopy. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (C) shows segmental scarring. Neither has a spike and dome pattern.

q: A 12-year-old child with a history of pyoderma two weeks earlier was evaluated and found to have hematuria with a serum creatinine level of 2 mg%. On follow-up three weeks later, the creatinine level increased to 4.5 mg%. Which of the following electron microscopy findings is most likely in this patient?
ex: Subepithelial deposit This clinical scenario describes an acute nephritic syndrome (hematuria, rising creatinine) following a skin infection (pyoderma), which is a classic presentation of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). The question asks for the finding on electron microscopy (EM). The pathognomonic ultrastructural feature of PSGN is the presence of large, discrete, hump-shaped, electron-dense immune complex deposits on the epithelial side of the glomerular basement membrane. These are referred to as subepithelial deposits or humps. While the rapidly worsening renal function suggests the development of a crescentic glomerulonephritis, crescents (C) are a finding on light microscopy, not EM. Subendothelial deposits (B) and intramembranous deposits (D) are characteristic of other types of glomerulonephritis.

q: A patient with elevated uric acid levels is receiving treatment for gout. Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the synthesis of uric acid?
ex: Allopurinol Uric acid is the final product of purine metabolism. The enzyme xanthine oxidase catalyzes the last two steps of this pathway. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. By blocking this enzyme, allopurinol decreases the production of uric acid, thereby lowering serum uric acid levels and preventing gout attacks. It is a first-line medication for the chronic management of gout. In contrast, probenecid (A) is a uricosuric agent that works by increasing the excretion of uric acid by the kidneys. Colchicine (C) and diclofenac (D) are anti-inflammatory drugs used to treat the pain and inflammation of an acute gout flare, but they do not alter uric acid levels.

q: A patient receiving digoxin developed toxicity, with a serum digoxin level of 4 ng/mL. Given that digoxin has a half-life of 40 hours, how long will it take for the drug concentration to decrease to the therapeutic level of 1 ng/mL?
ex: 80 hours A drugs half-life is the time it takes for its plasma concentration to decrease by 50%. The initial toxic concentration is 4 ng/ml, and the target is 1 ng/ml. After the first half-life (40 hours), the concentration will fall from 4 ng/ml to 2 ng/ml. After the second half-life (another 40 hours), the concentration will fall again by half, from 2 ng/ml to 1 ng/ml. To get from 4 ng/ml to 1 ng/ml requires two half-lives. Total time = 2 half-lives × 40 hours/half-life = 80 hours.

q: A patient undergoing cancer chemotherapy developed thrombocytopenia. Which of the following drugs is used to promote recovery from chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia?
ex: Oprelvekin Chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count) can be treated with thrombopoietic growth factors that stimulate platelet production in the bone marrow. Oprelvekin is a recombinant form of interleukin-11 (IL-11), a cytokine that stimulates the proliferation of hematopoietic progenitor cells and the maturation of megakaryocytes, the cells that produce platelets. This leads to an increase in the peripheral platelet count. Epoetin (A) is erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production. Filgrastim (C) is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that stimulates neutrophil production. Amifostine (D) is a cytoprotective agent used to reduce certain toxicities of chemotherapy but does not stimulate hematopoiesis.

q: Which of the following drugs acts as both an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and a neprilysin inhibitor?
ex: Omapatrilat Omapatrilat is a vasopeptidase inhibitor, a class of drugs designed to inhibit both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and neprilysin simultaneously. By inhibiting ACE, it reduces the production of the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. By inhibiting neprilysin, it increases the levels of vasodilating natriuretic peptides. This dual action provides potent blood pressure reduction. Sacubitril (B) is a neprilysin inhibitor, but it is combined with an angiotensin receptor blocker (valsartan), not an ACE inhibitor, to avoid the high incidence of angioedema associated with omapatrilat. Enalapril (C) is solely an ACE inhibitor, and candesartan (D) is an angiotensin receptor blocker.

q: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatigability. The mother reports that the child becomes very hungry between meals but recovers after eating. Liver examination shows no glycogen storage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Glycogen synthase The clinical presentation of fasting hypoglycemia (fatigue and hunger between meals) that is relieved by feeding, combined with the definitive finding of an absence of glycogen in the liver, points to a defect in glycogen synthesis. The key enzyme responsible for creating glycogen from glucose is glycogen synthase. A deficiency in this enzyme (Glycogen Storage Disease Type 0) means the liver cannot store glucose as glycogen after a meal. As a result, during a fast, the liver has no glycogen stores to break down (glycogenolysis) to maintain blood glucose levels, leading to hypoglycemia. Deficiencies in branching (A) or debranching (B) enzymes lead to abnormal glycogen structures, not absence. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (C) leads to a massive accumulation of normal glycogen.

q: A 35-year-old man presents with fatigue and weakness. Peripheral blood smear shows the findings illustrated below. What is the most likely genetic change associated with this patient?
ex: T(15,17) The peripheral blood smear in the image shows numerous abnormal promyelocytes containing heavy cytoplasmic granules and likely Auer rods. This appearance is characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. Patients with APL commonly present with symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, anemia, and bleeding tendencies due to bone marrow failure and coagulopathy. The most common genetic abnormality associated with APL is the translocation t(15;17). This translocation occurs between chromosome 15 and chromosome 17 and results in the fusion of the PML gene on chromosome 15 with the RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) gene on chromosome 17. The resulting PML-RARA fusion protein blocks the normal differentiation of myeloid precursor cells at the promyelocyte stage, leading to accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. This genetic defect is clinically important because APL is highly responsive to targeted therapy. Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) or arsenic trioxide helps overcome the differentiation block, allowing the leukemic promyelocytes to mature into normal cells. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) t(15;17), which is the hallmark cytogenetic abnormality of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia.

q: A 44-year-old patient presents with lymphadenopathy. On examination, generalized lymphadenopathy is noted without organomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows lymphocytosis with smudge cells. What is the next appropriate step in the diagnostic workup?
ex: Flow cytometry This clinical presentation is highly characteristic of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), a malignancy of mature B-lymphocytes. Key features include an older patient, generalized lymphadenopathy, significant lymphocytosis, and the presence of smudge cells (fragile neoplastic lymphocytes) on the peripheral smear. The gold standard and essential next step to confirm the diagnosis is immunophenotyping by flow cytometry on the peripheral blood. This test identifies a monoclonal population of B-cells expressing a unique pattern of surface markers (typically CD19, CD20-dim, CD5, and CD23). This confirms the clonality and specific cell type, establishing the diagnosis of CLL without initially needing more invasive procedures like a bone marrow (BM) examination or lymph node biopsy, which are reserved for atypical cases or staging.

q: A 7-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with swelling of the jaw. On examination, cytopenias are noted, and bone marrow aspiration shows the cells depicted below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Burkitts lymphoma This combination of features—a jaw mass in a child (a classic location for endemic Burkitts), cytopenias indicating bone marrow infiltration, and the characteristic cell morphology—is pathognomonic for Burkitts lymphoma/leukemia. The bone marrow aspirate shows uniform, medium-sized lymphoblasts with round nuclei, stippled chromatin, and, most distinctively, intensely basophilic cytoplasm filled with prominent lipid vacuoles. This morphology is classified as L3 in the FAB system. Burkitts lymphoma is an extremely aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Follicular lymphoma (A) is a low-grade lymphoma typically found in adults. Adult T-cell leukemia (B) is also rare in children. Infectious mononucleosis (D) features reactive atypical lymphocytes, not a uniform population of malignant blasts.

q: Identify the structure in the below histology slide?
ex: Glomerulus The histology slide clearly shows the microscopic architecture of the kidney cortex. The prominent, ball-like structures are glomeruli, which are tufts of capillaries responsible for the initial filtration of blood. Each glomerulus is surrounded by Bowmans capsule and is interspersed among numerous cross-sections of renal tubules. This appearance is uniquely characteristic of the kidney. Islets of Langerhans (A) are endocrine cell clusters found in the pancreas. A lymph node (C) has a distinct architecture with follicles and sinuses. Hassalls corpuscles (D) are structures found only in the medulla of the thymus. The image is unequivocally a view of the renal cortex, and the identified structures are glomeruli.

q: Which of the following statements are true regarding the relative risk associated with Mendelian patterns of inheritance?
ex: 1/4 autosomal recessive This question asks for the correct recurrence risk for an affected child in a typical Mendelian inheritance scenario. For an autosomal recessive disorder, an affected child (genotype aa) is most commonly born to two heterozygous carrier parents (genotype Aa). In such a cross (Aa x Aa), the probability for each pregnancy is as follows: a 1 in 4 chance of having an affected child (aa), a 2 in 4 (or 1/2) chance of having an unaffected carrier child (Aa), and a 1 in 4 chance of having an unaffected, non-carrier child (AA). Therefore, the risk of having another child affected with the same autosomal recessive condition is 1/4 or 25%. The other options are incorrect for standard Mendelian patterns. q: A sample collected from the perineal region of a 10-year-old child was tested using picric acid and showed yellow, needle-shaped crystals. Which diagnostic test is this?
ex: Barberios test This question describes a presumptive forensic test for the identification of semen. Barberios test utilizes a saturated solution of picric acid. When this reagent is mixed with a sample containing seminal fluid, the picric acid reacts with spermine, a substance found in high concentration in semen. This chemical reaction results in the formation of spermine picrate crystals. As described in the question, these crystals have a characteristic appearance: they are yellow and needle-shaped. The formation of these specific crystals is considered a positive result and is strong presumptive evidence for the presence of semen. The other options are different forensic tests: the Florence test (C) detects choline, the acid phosphatase test (B) detects an enzyme in semen, and the Teichmann test (D) is for blood.

q: Which autopsy technique is used to minimize the risk of infection transmission in patients with HIV?
ex: Letulle technique The Letulle technique is an autopsy method in which all thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic organs are removed together as a single organ block and then dissected outside the body. This technique minimizes repeated handling of individual organs within the body cavity and reduces the number of cuts and manipulations required during the initial stages of the autopsy. Because of this, it helps reduce the exposure of the pathologist to blood, body fluids, and potentially infectious materials. In patients with HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or other blood-borne infections, minimizing direct exposure to infected tissues is extremely important. The Letulle technique allows the organs to be examined in a controlled manner after removal, which lowers the risk of accidental injuries, splashes, and aerosol generation that could transmit infection. Other techniques are less suitable in such situations. The Virchow technique removes organs one by one, increasing handling and exposure. The Rokitansky technique involves in-situ dissection, and the Ghon technique removes organs in functional blocks but still requires more manipulation. Therefore, the Letulle technique is preferred to minimize infection transmission risk during autopsy in HIV patients.

q: In a deceased individual, the body temperature was recorded as 39°C. What is the most likely cause of death?
ex: Septicemia Normally, a body cools after death (algor mortis). However, in certain conditions, the body temperature can remain elevated or even rise for a short period postmortem, a phenomenon called postmortem caloricity. This occurs in deaths associated with a hypermetabolic state or excessive heat production immediately prior to death. Septicemia (sepsis) is a classic cause. The massive systemic inflammatory response in sepsis generates a high antemortem fever, and continued metabolic activity of bacteria after death can contribute to this sustained high temperature. Other causes include heat stroke, certain poisonings (like strychnine), and pontine hemorrhage. Conditions like hemorrhage (D) and cyanide poisoning (A) typically lead to rapid body cooling.

q: Which autopsy technique involves the en bloc removal of the thoracic, cervical, and abdominal organs together?
ex: Lettuce technique The autopsy method that involves removing the thoracic, cervical, and abdominal organs as a single, large unit is known as the Letulle technique. This is also referred to as the en masse or en bloc method. By keeping all the organ systems connected, this technique allows for excellent examination of anatomical relationships, which is particularly useful for tracing the pathways of trauma, metastatic cancer, or complex congenital anomalies. The Virchow technique (B) involves removing organs one by one. The Rokitansky technique (A) is an in situ dissection. The Ghon technique (D) involves removal by functional blocks (e.g., thoraco-cervical block, abdominal block). Lettuce is likely a common misspelling of Letulle.

q: During the harvest season, a farmer resting in the shade felt a sudden bite and saw the creature move away quickly. He later developed drowsiness, pain, and uncontrolled bleeding, and the bite site became red with blister formation. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
ex: Viper The clinical syndrome described is classic for envenomation by a viper snake (such as a Russells viper or saw-scaled viper), which are common in agricultural areas. Viper venom is primarily hemotoxic and cytotoxic. This leads to the characteristic local signs of severe pain, redness, swelling, and blister formation. Systemically, the hemotoxin causes a profound coagulopathy by consuming clotting factors, which manifests as uncontrolled bleeding from the bite site and other areas. Drowsiness can result from systemic toxicity and hypotension. In contrast, krait venom (D) is primarily neurotoxic, causing paralysis with minimal local signs. Scorpion stings (A) and wasp stings (C) cause local pain and potential allergic reactions but do not cause this type of bleeding disorder.

q: A patient developed seizures, muscle tremors, and backward arching of the spine after consuming a herbal medicine. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
ex: Strychnine poisoning This constellation of symptoms is pathognomonic for strychnine poisoning. Strychnine is a potent neurotoxin, sometimes found as an adulterant in herbal medicines or in rodenticides. It acts as a competitive antagonist of the inhibitory neurotransmitter glycine in the spinal cord and brainstem. By blocking this inhibition, strychnine causes uncontrolled, exaggerated reflex neuronal activity. This leads to characteristic and severe muscular convulsions, tremors, and opisthotonus (a dramatic, rigid arching of the back, causing a backward aching of the spine). The seizures are often intensely painful and can be triggered by even minor stimuli. Oleander (B) is cardiotoxic, Aconite (C) causes arrhythmias and paresthesias, and Castor seeds (D) cause severe gastrointestinal distress.

q: A 45-year-old man presented to the outpatient department with abdominal pain and diarrhea for the past three days, along with fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss. On examination, his blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg with a regular pulse of 70 beats per minute, and he was found to have jaundice. Ultrasonography of the liver showed intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile duct dilatation with strictures and intraductal pigmented stones. What is the most likely causative agent?
ex: Clonorchis sinensis The clinical and radiological findings are highly suggestive of chronic biliary disease caused by the Chinese liver fluke, Clonorchis sinensis. This parasitic flatworm infects the biliary tree. Chronic infection leads to persistent inflammation of the bile ducts, causing periductal fibrosis, ductal strictures, and both intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary dilatation. This chronic inflammation and stasis also promote the formation of intraductal pigmented stones. The patients symptoms of abdominal pain, jaundice, and weight loss are consistent with biliary obstruction and its complications, which include recurrent pyogenic cholangitis and an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. The other parasites listed are intestinal nematodes and do not cause this specific biliary pathology.

q: A sewer worker presented with high-grade fever, jaundice, and conjunctival suffusion. What is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
ex: Microscopic agglutination test The classic triad of fever, jaundice, and conjunctival suffusion (redness of the conjunctiva without pus) in a patient with an occupational risk like being a sewer worker is highly indicative of Weils disease, the severe form of leptospirosis. This is a zoonotic infection caused by the spirochete Leptospira. The definitive and gold standard serological test for diagnosing leptospirosis is the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT). This complex test detects antibodies in the patients serum that react with live Leptospira serovars. A four-fold or greater rise in the MAT titer between acute and convalescent serum samples confirms the diagnosis. The other tests are for different diseases: Paul-Bunnell for infectious mononucleosis (B), Widal for typhoid fever (C), and Weil-Felix for rickettsial diseases (D).

q: Boys hostel get infected as hostlers develop polymorphous rashes with fever?

Chickenpox commonly spreads rapidly in crowded settings such as hostels, schools, and dormitories through respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicular lesions. A key clinical feature of chickenpox is a polymorphous rash, meaning lesions are present in different stages simultaneously (macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts). Fever, malaise, and itching usually accompany the rash. Management focuses on preventing transmission and reducing viral replication. Patients should be isolated for about 6 days, typically until the lesions begin to crust over, as infectivity is highest from 1–2 days before rash appearance until crusting occurs. The antiviral drug Acyclovir is used to inhibit viral DNA replication. Early administration helps reduce severity, duration of fever, and formation of new lesions, especially during outbreaks in closed communities like hostels. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is generally reserved for immuno compromised individuals or severe cases, not routine outbreaks. Therefore, the most appropriate management in this scenario is isolation for 6 days with acyclovir therapy.

q: Rotavirus diagnosis?
ex: Antigen in stool Rotavirus is a leading cause of severe acute gastroenteritis in infants and young children. For diagnosing an active infection, the most widely used, rapid, and reliable method is the detection of viral antigen in a stool sample. This is typically performed using commercial enzyme-linked immuno sorbent assay (ELISA) kits or latex agglutination tests. These assays are highly sensitive and specific for detecting a common rotavirus structural protein (VP6), confirming that the virus is actively replicating in the gut and is the cause of the diarrhea. Serology (C) is not useful for acute diagnosis. Antibody detection in stool (B) is not a standard method. Viruses cannot be seen with light microscopy (D).

q: What is true for trichomonas?
o: Twitching motility is seen on wet mount

ex: Twitching motility is seen on wet mount Trichomonas vaginalis, the protozoan parasite responsible for trichomoniasis, exists only in a trophozoite stage and does not form cysts (D is incorrect)5. A key diagnostic feature is its appearance on a saline wet mount of vaginal or urethral discharge. Under the microscope, the pear-shaped trophozoite exhibits a characteristic and vigorous jerky or twitching motility, which is due to the rapid movement of its flagellar. This feature is highly specific and allows for a rapid diagnosis. While it can be grown in special media like Diamonds medium, this is not routine (B is incorrect)7. Darting motility (C) is a term more commonly used to describe the movement of bacteria like Vibrio cholerae, not Trichomonas. Therefore, the observation of its unique twitching movement on a wet mount is a true and classic diagnostic sign.

q: A child presented with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed low glucose levels and gram-negative pleomorphic organisms. What is the characteristic feature of this organism on culture?
o: Satellitism in presence of Staphylococcus aureus
Non lactose fermentation on Mc Conkey agar
ex: Satellitism in presence of Staphylococcus aureus The clinical presentation of meningitis in a child, with CSF findings of low glucose and gram-negative pleomorphic rods, is highly suggestive of infection with Haemophilus influenzae. This bacterium is fastidious and requires two specific growth factors: X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD). Standard sheep blood agar provides X factor but not V factor. However, Staphylococcus aureus produces V factor as a metabolic by product. When both organisms are plated on blood agar, H. influenzae will only grow in tiny colonies immediately surrounding the larger S. aureus colonies, which are supplying the needed V factor. This phenomenon is known as satellitism and is a classic laboratory test for identifying H. influenzae. The other options describe different bacteria: alpha hemolysis (A) is typical of S. pneumoniae, non-lactose fermentation (C) is seen in Salmonella, and bacitracin sensitivity (D) identifies S. pyogenes.

q: A patient presenting with fever and swelling tested positive for filarial antigen. What should be the next step in management?
o: Peripheral blood smear to identify microfilaria
ex: Peripheral blood smear to identify microfilaria The detection of filarial antigen in the blood is a highly sensitive and specific method for diagnosing lymphatic filariasis, particularly that caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. A positive antigen test is considered diagnostic, and in most clinical settings, treatment would be the next step. However, among the given options, which are all further diagnostic tests, the most logical traditional step would be to attempt to visualize the parasite itself. This is done by examining a peripheral blood smear for the presence of microfilariae. Since the microfilariae of W. bancrofti exhibit nocturnal periodicity (they are most numerous in peripheral blood at night), a nighttime blood draw is preferred. A DEC provocation test (A) is a method used to stimulate the release of microfilariae into the bloodstream during the daytime to facilitate their detection on a smear.

q: A patient presented with hepatosplenomegaly and was found to have pallor on examination. A rapid antigen test was positive for HRP- 2 antigen. Which species of Plasmodium is responsible for this infection?
ex: Falciparum Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for malaria work by detecting specific antigens produced by the Plasmodium parasites. The Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP-2) antigen is produced exclusively by Plasmodium falciparum. Therefore, a positive result for HRP-2 is diagnostic for an infection with P. falciparum. Other RDTs may detect different antigens, such as plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH), which can be pan-specific (detecting all species) or specific to other species like P. vivax. However, the finding of a positive HRP-2 antigen test, as in this patient, specifically identifies the causative agent as P. falciparum. The clinical findings of hepatosplenomegaly and pallor (due to anemia from hemolysis) are also consistent with a significant malarial infection.

q: A man from Bihar presented with fever and skin lesions. Microscopic examination revealed an organism containing a kinetoplast. What is the causative agent responsible for this condition?
ex: Leishmania tropica The key to this diagnosis is the geographical location and the microscopic finding. Bihar is a well-known endemic region for visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) in India. The microscopic finding of an organism with a kinetoplast is a defining characteristic of protozoa belonging to the order Kinetoplastida, which includes both Leishmania and Trypanosoma. The kinetoplast is a distinctive network of mitochondrial DNA located within a single large mitochondrion. In a patient from Bihar presenting with fever and skin lesions (which can occur in post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis), finding a kinetoplast-containing organism is diagnostic of Leishmania. Toxoplasma, Babesia, and Plasmodium (Malaria) are all protozoan parasites, but they do not possess a kinetoplast. Leishmania tropica is a species that causes cutaneous leishmaniasis.

q: A patient with a history of multiple sexual partners presented with fever and jaundice. Laboratory investigations showed elevated SGPT levels, and both HBsAg and HBeAg were positive. Which of the following treatment options is not recommended in this condition?
ex: Combination of peg interferon + lamivudine The patient has acute hepatitis B, indicated by fever, jaundice, and high SGPT. The serology shows HBsAg positive (infection) and HBeAg positive (high viral replication and high infectivity). Treatment for chronic hepatitis B includes nucleos(t)ide analogs like lamivudine and tenofovir, or immunomodulators like pegylated interferon. However, combination therapy with both pegylated interferon and lamivudine is generally not recommended. Clinical trials have shown that this combination does not provide a significant benefit over monotherapy with either agent alone and may increase the risk of side effects. While both drugs are used individually, their concurrent use is not a standard of care. Therefore, this combination would be the treatment that is not recommended for this patient.

q: Owl eye inclusion bodies?
ex: CMV The presence of owls eye inclusion bodies is a pathognomonic histological finding for infection with Cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. These characteristic inclusions are seen within infected cells, which become markedly enlarged (cytomegaly). The inclusion itself is a large, basophilic, intranuclear body that is surrounded by a clear halo. This appearance, with the central dark inclusion (the pupil) and the surrounding clear zone (the iris), strikingly resembles the eye of an owl. These inclusions can be found in various tissues, including the lungs, kidneys, liver, and gastrointestinal tract, in patients with active CMV infection, particularly those who are immuno compromised. The other pathogens listed are associated with different histological findings.

q: A 50-year-old man from Delhi presented with fever, headache, joint pain, petechial rash, and bleeding gums. Blood investigations revealed hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 3,000/mm³, and a platelet count of 20,000/ mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Dengue The combination of symptoms and laboratory findings is highly characteristic of Dengue fever, an arboviral infection endemic in areas like Delhi. The clinical features include high-grade fever, headache, and severe joint pain (myalgias and arthralgias, giving it the name break-bone fever). The presence of a petechial rash and bleeding gums are warning signs of severe dengue, indicating increased vascular permeability. The laboratory results are classic for dengue: leukopenia (WBC-3000) and severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 20,000). This triad of fever, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic manifestations is the hallmark of dengue. Scrub typhus, typhoid, and babesiosis can present with fever and cytopenias but this specific constellation, especially the severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding, strongly points to dengue.

q: A patient presented with a painless genital ulcer accompanied by non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Syphilis The classic presentation of primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, is a single, painless ulcer (known as a chancre) at the site of inoculation. The chancre typically has a clean base and firm, indurated borders. This is often accompanied by regional non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. This combination of a painless ulcer and non-tender nodes is highly specific for primary syphilis. In contrast, chancroid (B), caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, typically presents with multiple, painful ulcers and tender, suppurative lymphadenopathy (buboes). Granuloma inguinale (C) causes painless, progressive, ulcerative lesions without significant lymphadenopathy. NODIA 240=== page 234 Examination Paper 2023

q: A patient with a history of multiple sexual partners presented with urethral discharge. Gram staining of the discharge showed characteristic findings. Which of the following drugs is not used in the management of this condition?
ex: Ampicillin The image shows a Gram stain of urethral discharge with gram-negative diplococci located inside polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils). This is the classic microscopic finding for urethritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Due to widespread and high-level resistance, penicillins, including ampicillin, are no longer effective and are not used in the management of gonorrhea. The current recommended treatment is ceftriaxone. Often, treatment also includes an agent to cover for potential co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, such as azithromycin or doxycycline, both of which are effective options. Therefore, ampicillin is the only drug on the list that is not a part of modern treatment regimens for this condition.

q: An HIV-positive patient presented with pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was negative on KOH wet mount, but Gomori methenamine silver staining revealed crescent- shaped, black-colored cysts. The organism was found to be non-cultivable. What is the most likely causative organism?
ex: Pneumocystis This scenario is classic for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), a common opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. The organism, Pneumocystis jirovecii, is a fungus that cannot be grown in standard laboratory culture (it is non-cultivable). A KOH wet mount, used for detecting many fungi, is typically negative. The definitive diagnosis is made by visualizing the organism in a respiratory sample, such as from a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). The Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain is the classic method used, which stains the cyst walls of Pneumocystis a distinct black or dark brown color. The cysts often appear as crushed, crescent-shaped, or circular structures, matching the description perfectly.

q: A 10-year-old child presented to the outpatient department. According to the National Immunization Schedule, which vaccine should be advised at this age?
ex: Td vaccine According to Indias National Immunization Schedule (NIS), several vaccines are administered during infancy and early childhood. By the age of 5, a child should have received booster doses of DPT (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus). The schedule then includes further booster doses at later ages to maintain immunity. At 10 years of age, and again at 16 years, a booster dose of the Td vaccine (Tetanus and diphtheria, adult formulation) is recommended. The adult formulation (Td) contains a lower dose of the diphtheria toxoid compared to the pediatric DPT vaccine. BCG is given at birth. The second DPT booster is given at 5 years. Typhoid vaccine is recommended but may have different schedules depending on the type used. The Td vaccine is the specifically scheduled vaccine for a 10-year-old.

q: A 22-year-old pregnant woman presented to a subcentre with a history of consuming papaya and feared that it might have caused abortion. After thorough examination, the pregnancy was found to be safe, and she was reassured and sent home. Which health worker should be sent for a rural home visit in this situation?
ex: Anganwadi worker In rural health services under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, the Anganwadi Worker plays an important role in providing maternal and child health education, nutritional guidance, and counseling at the community level. In this case, the pregnant woman was worried that consuming papaya might lead to abortion. After medical examination, the pregnancy was found to be safe and she was reassured. However, myths and misconceptions related to diet during pregnancy are common in rural communities. A home visit is useful to reinforce counseling, provide reassurance, and educate the woman and her family about safe nutrition during pregnancy. The Anganwadi worker regularly conducts home visits, nutrition education sessions, and antenatal counseling, making her the most appropriate worker for follow-up in this situation. Other options are less suitable. Accredited Social Health Activist mainly focuses on mobilizing people for health services and institutional delivery, while a trained birth attendant assists during delivery. The medical officer (MO) is responsible for clinical care at health facilities rather than routine household counseling. Thus, the Anganwadi worker is the appropriate health worker for the rural home visit.

q: A study was conducted comparing two groups from the same aniline dye factory: workers directly involved in factory operations for 20 years and office workers from the same factory. What type of study design does this represent?
ex: Retrospective cohort study This study design starts by defining two groups (cohorts) based on their past exposure status and then looks forward in time (from records) to ascertain outcome. One group was exposed to aniline dye in the factory, and the other group (office workers in the same factory) was not. The study then presumably assesses the incidence of a disease (like bladder cancer) in both groups over a 20-year period. Since the exposures and outcomes have all occurred in the past and the investigator is using existing records to assemble the cohorts and determine their outcomes, this is a retrospective cohort study. It is not a prospective cohort study because the investigator is not following the groups forward in real-time. It is not a case-control study because the groups are defined by exposure, not by disease status.

q: How to collect tap water for bacteriological study
o: Before collecting water let water flow for 1 min
Attach bottle before turning on the tap to avoid splashing
Attach bottle to mid stream & avoid splashing
ex: Attach bottle to mid stream & avoid splashing The correct procedure for collecting a tap water sample for bacteriological analysis is designed to ensure the sample is representative of the water in the main pipe and is not contaminated by the tap itself. The standard procedure involves several steps. First, the tap should be cleaned and sterilized (often by flaming). Then, the water should be allowed to run at a medium flow for 2-3 minutes to flush out any stagnant water from the local pipes. Finally, the sterile collection bottle should be opened carefully, and the sample should be collected from the mid-stream of the water flow without the bottle touching the tap and without splashing, which could introduce contaminants. The bottle should not be completely filled to allow for mixing before analysis. Option C best describes the collection part of this process.

q: What is the best measure for assessing the overall health status of a community, and which indicator is most sensitive to the availability and utilization of health services?
ex: IMR The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR), which is the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births, is widely regarded as one of the most sensitive indicators of the overall health status of a community. It reflects not just the health of infants but also the socioeconomic conditions, public health infrastructure, and the quality and accessibility of maternal and child health services. A high IMR suggests issues with nutrition, sanitation, infectious disease control, and poor access to or utilization of healthcare. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) is specific to maternal health. DALYs measure the burden of disease , and the HDI is a broader measure of development that includes education and income, not just health. IMR is particularly sensitive to changes in the healthcare system.

q: Which of the following statements regarding the Colombo Plan is correct?

ex: Mannitol Dialysis Disequilibrium Syndrome (DDS) is a neurological complication resulting from cerebral edema. It occurs when hemodialysis removes urea from the blood much faster than from the brain, creating an osmotic gradient that pulls water into the brain cells. The treatment aims to counteract this osmotic shift. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic. When administered intravenously, it increases the osmolarity of the blood, creating a reverse osmotic gradient that pulls fluid out of the brain tissue and into the vasculature, thereby reducing cerebral edema and intracranial pressure. Loop diuretics like ethacrynic acid (A) and bumetanide (D) do not address the central osmotic imbalance. Aspirin (C) has no role in this condition.

q: A patient is scheduled to undergo cardiac surgery. Which antibiotic is most appropriate for preoperative prophylaxis?
ex: Cefazolin The goal of preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis for cardiac surgery is to prevent surgical site infections (SSIs), which are most commonly caused by skin flora like Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Cefazolin, a first-generation cephalosporin, is the recommended drug of choice for this indication. It has an excellent spectrum of activity against these common pathogens, a good safety profile, and appropriate pharmacokinetics to maintain adequate tissue levels during surgery. It is typically administered intravenously within 60 minutes prior to the initial incision. The other antibiotics listed either have an inappropriate spectrum of coverage for skin flora or are associated with higher rates of resistance, making them suboptimal choices for this specific prophylactic use.

q: A child presented with confusion and irritability, had not passed urine since morning, complained of photophobia, and had a history of eating something while playing in the field. What is the most likely type of poisoning, and what is the appropriate antidote?
ex: Datura-physostigmine The combination of central nervous system effects (confusion, irritability), urinary retention, and photophobia (from mydriasis) is characteristic of an anticholinergic toxidrome. A common plant source for this poisoning is Datura (Jimsonweed). The appropriate antidote for severe anticholinergic poisoning with central effects is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that can cross the blood-brain barrier. Physostigmine is a tertiary amine, allowing it to penetrate the CNS and reverse both central and peripheral symptoms. Pyridostigmine (A) is a quaternary amine that does not cross the blood-brain barrier and is therefore ineffective for the CNS symptoms. Yellow oleander (C, D) is a cardiac glycoside, and pralidoxime is an antidote for organophosphate poisoning.

q: A patient with organophosphate poisoning was treated with atropine infusion and pralidoxime. Two hours later, the patient developed a high- grade fever. What is the most likely cause of this fever?
ex: Side effects of atropine In the treatment of organophosphate (OP) poisoning, high doses of atropine are administered to block the muscarinic effects of excess acetylcholine. A significant anticholinergic side effect of atropine is the inhibition of sweating (anhidrosis) by blocking muscarinic receptors on sweat glands. The inability to sweat severely impairs the bodys ability to dissipate heat, which can lead to a rise in core body temperature, a condition known as atropine fever. This is a direct pharmacological consequence of the high-dose atropine therapy required in this setting. The fever is not a typical effect of pralidoxime (A) or the OP poisoning itself (C), and increased secretions (D) would cause heat loss, not fever.

q: What is the treatment of Aspirin overdose?
ex: IV NaHCO3 The primary goals in managing aspirin (salicylate) overdose are to correct metabolic disturbances and enhance the drugs elimination. This is best achieved with intravenous sodium bicarbonate (IV NaHCO3). Administering bicarbonate alkalinizes the urine (raises its pH). Since aspirin is a weak acid, a more alkaline urine causes the aspirin molecules to become ionized. This ion trapping prevents them from being reabsorbed across the renal tubular membranes, thereby significantly increasing their excretion. Additionally, IV bicarbonate helps to correct the severe metabolic acidosis that is a hallmark of significant salicylate toxicity. N-Acetylcysteine (B) is the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose, not aspirin.

q: A patient with psychosis was being treated with haloperidol but showed inadequate response. A new drug was added, after which the patient developed adverse effects such as increased salivation and dyslipidemia. Which drug is most likely to have been prescribed?
ex: Clozapine The clinical scenario describes a patient with treatment-resistant psychosis, as evidenced by the lack of response to haloperidol. Clozapine is the gold-standard antipsychotic for such cases. Furthermore, clozapine has a unique side-effect profile that matches the description perfectly. It is well-known for causing significant metabolic side effects, including weight gain and dyslipidemia. Most distinctively, unlike other antipsychotics that often cause dry mouth, clozapine frequently causes marked sialorrhea (increased salivation). This combination of use in treatment-resistant cases and the specific adverse effects of sialorrhea and dyslipidemia is highly characteristic of clozapine, making it the most likely new drug.

q: A patient with bronchial asthma on inhaled corticosteroid therapy presented with oral thrush. Which antifungal drug is used for its management?
ex: Clotrimazole Oropharyngeal candidiasis, commonly known as oral thrush, is a frequent local side effect of inhaled corticosteroids due to local immune suppression. The standard treatment for uncomplicated cases is a topical antifungal agent. Clotrimazole is an excellent choice as it is available in the form of a troche (lozenge). The patient dissolves the troche slowly in the mouth, which allows for prolonged contact between the antifungal medication and the affected oral and pharyngeal mucosa, leading to effective eradication of the Candida infection. Griseofulvin (D) and terbinafine (A) are not effective against Candida. Flucytosine (B) is a systemic antifungal reserved for severe, life-threatening fungal infections and is not used for oral thrush.

q: What is the mechanism of action of t PA?
ex: Fibrinolytic effect t-PA stands for tissue Plasminogen Activator. It is a proteolytic enzyme that plays a crucial role in dissolving blood clots. Its mechanism of action is fibrinolytic. t-PA functions by binding to fibrin within an existing thrombus (blood clot). This binding activates t-PA, enabling it to convert plasminogen, an inactive proenzyme that is also present in the clot, into its active form, plasmin. Plasmin is a potent enzyme that directly degrades the fibrin meshwork which forms the structural integrity of the clot. This enzymatic breakdown of fibrin leads to the dissolution of the clot. t-PA does not prevent clot formation (C) or have direct anti-platelet (D) or anti-thrombin (A) effects; it actively breaks down a pre-formed clot.

q: A child diagnosed with whooping cough has a total leukocyte count greater than 50,000 cells/ mm³ with absolute lymphocytosis. What is the appropriate treatment?

A very high total leukocyte count (TLC) with a predominance of lymphocytes is a hallmark of severe pertussis and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. The drugs of choice for treating pertussis are macrolide antibiotics. Azithromycin is the preferred agent, particularly in infants and children, due to its once-daily dosing, shorter 5-day course, and superior safety profile compared to older macrolides like erythromycin. While clarithromycin (A) is an alternative, azithromycin is generally favored. Antibiotic treatment is crucial to eradicate the organism, thereby reducing the patients infectivity and preventing further spread. If started early, it may also lessen the severity and duration of symptoms. Ampicillin (B) and cotrimoxazole (C) are not effective first-line treatments.

q: Drug of Choice for Gonnorhea?
ex: Ceftriaxone The treatment for gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, has been complicated by the bacteriums ability to develop widespread resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics. Due to high rates of resistance, penicillins (like ampicillin), tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended. Current treatment guidelines from major public health bodies like the CDC recommend a single intramuscular injection of Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, as the primary and most reliable treatment for uncomplicated urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhea. For many years, it was combined with azithromycin, but due to increasing azithromycin resistance, ceftriaxone remains the cornerstone of therapy. Clarithromycin (A) is not used for treating gonorrhea.

q: A patient being treated with crinoline for hypertension and using nicotine replacement therapy suddenly stopped taking crinoline and developed a headache. What is the underlying mechanism responsible for this headache?
ex: Rebound hypertension Clonidine lowers blood pressure by stimulating central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which suppresses sympathetic nervous system outflow. When clonidine is taken chronically, the body adapts to this state of reduced sympathetic tone. If the medication is stopped abruptly, this inhibitory effect is suddenly removed. The result is a surge in sympathetic activity, leading to a rapid and often severe increase in blood pressure to levels that can exceed the pre-treatment baseline. This phenomenon is known as rebound hypertension. A severe, acute headache is a very common symptom of this hypertensive crisis. While receptor down regulation (D) during treatment contributes to this withdrawal phenomenon, the direct cause of the headache is the rebound hypertension itself. q: Which disease is caused by zinc deficiency
ex: Acrodermatitis enteropathica Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare, autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by the inability to absorb zinc from the diet. It can also be acquired due to nutritional deficiencies. The condition classically presents in infancy after weaning from breast milk and manifests with a distinct clinical triad: 1) a periorificial (around the mouth and anus) and acral (on the hands and feet) dermatitis, 2) alopecia (hair loss), and 3) severe diarrhea. These symptoms are a direct result of profound zinc deficiency. The condition responds dramatically to oral zinc supplementation. While zinc deficiency can worsen other skin conditions, it is the direct and sole cause of acrodermatitis enteropathica. The other conditions listed have different etiologies.

q: A person who had low blood pressure during childhood is more likely to have low blood pressure in adulthood. What is this phenomenon called?
ex: Tracking phenomenon The tendency for a physiological variable, such as blood pressure or cholesterol levels, to remain in a certain percentile or rank over time as a person ages is known as the tracking phenomenon. The statement that a person with low blood pressure in childhood is likely to have relatively low blood pressure in adulthood is a direct example of this concept. Similarly, children with blood pressure in the higher percentiles are at an increased risk of developing hypertension as adults. This phenomenon highlights the importance of monitoring risk factors like blood pressure from an early age, as childhood values can be predictive of adult health status. The Rule of Halves refers to the underdiagnosis and undertreatment of hypertension in a community , while the WHO Steps approach is a framework for chronic disease surveillance.

q: Deficiency of which vitamin is the most common cause of petechial bleeding of the gums?
ex: Vit C Bleeding from the gums (gingival hemorrhage), often appearing as petechiae, is a hallmark sign of scurvy, the disease caused by severe Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency. Vitamin C is essential for the synthesis of collagen, a critical protein for maintaining the structural integrity of blood vessels and connective tissues. In a deficient state, capillary walls become fragile and are prone to rupture with minor trauma, leading to bleeding. The gums are particularly affected, becoming swollen, spongy, and friable. While Vitamin K deficiency can cause generalized bleeding due to impaired coagulation factor synthesis, the characteristic petechial bleeding specifically from inflamed gums is most strongly associated with Vitamin C deficiency.

q: A patient shows a negative Rinne test with 256 Hz and 512 Hz tuning forks but a positive Rinne test with a 1024 Hz tuning fork. What is the estimated air–bone gap in this patient?
ex: 30 to 45 Db Rinnes test compares air conduction (AC) and bone conduction (BC) of sound. A negative test (BC > AC) indicates a conductive hearing loss. The magnitude of the conductive loss, or the air-bone gap (ABG), correlates with which tuning fork frequencies give a negative result. A negative Rinne at 256 Hz corresponds to an ABG of at least 15-20 dB. A negative Rinne at 512 Hz corresponds to an ABG of at least 30-35 dB. A negative Rinne at 1024 Hz corresponds to an ABG of at least 45-50 dB. This patient is negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, but becomes positive at 1024 Hz. This means their air-bone gap is large enough to be detected by the 512 Hz fork but not large enough to be detected by the 1024 Hz fork. This places the air-bone gap in the range of 30 to 45 dB.

q: Identify the marked structure

The arrow is pointing to the slit-like recess or depression located just posterior and superior to this bulge. The tubal tonsil (A) is lymphoid tissue near the opening, and the Eustachian tube opening (C) is the orifice itself, anterior to the fossa.

q: An elderly patient presented with a change in voice and was diagnosed with cancer. He subsequently underwent a specific intervention. Following which surgical procedure is this intervention typically performed?
ex: Total Laryngectomy The device shown in the image is a tracheoesophageal voice prosthesis. This device is specifically used for voice rehabilitation after a total laryngectomy. During a total laryngectomy, the entire larynx (voice box) is removed, and the trachea is brought out to the neck to create a permanent stoma for breathing. This disconnects the lungs from the pharynx and mouth, resulting in the loss of normal speech. To restore voice, a small puncture can be created between the trachea and the esophagus, into which this one-way valve prosthesis is placed. It allows air from the lungs to be shunted into the esophagus, causing the pharyngoesophageal segment to vibrate and produce sound, which can then be articulated into speech. This intervention is not required for partial laryngectomies, where some portion of the larynx is preserved.

q: A 10-year-old child presented to the pediatric outpatient department with fever, rash, and Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Measles The clinical triad of fever, rash, and Kopliks spots is pathognomonic for measles (rubeola). Kopliks spots are small, white or bluish-white spots with an erythematous base, typically found on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars. They are an enanthem that appears 1-2 days before the characteristic maculopapular skin rash (exanthem) and are considered a definitive sign of measles. The rash typically starts on the face and spreads downwards. Mumps is characterized by parotitis , rubella has a milder rash and lymphadenopathy , and chickenpox presents with a vesicular rash. The presence of Kopliks spots makes the diagnosis of measles certain.

q: Identify the vitamin deficiency in the child shown in the image below.
ex: Vit D Deficiency The image shows bowing of the legs (genu varum) in a child, which is a classic sign of Rickets caused by Vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D plays a crucial role in the absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine, which are essential for proper bone mineralization and skeletal growth. When vitamin D levels are insufficient, bones become soft, weak, and poorly mineralized, leading to skeletal deformities. In growing children, this defective mineralization affects the epiphyseal growth plates, causing characteristic features such as bowed legs, knock knees, widening of wrists and ankles, frontal bossing, and rachitic rosary (enlargement at the costochondral junctions). The bowing of legs occurs because the softened bones cannot withstand the body weight during standing and walking. Common causes include inadequate sunlight exposure, poor dietary intake of vitamin D, malnutrition, and malabsorption disorders. Early diagnosis and treatment with vitamin D supplementation and adequate sunlight exposure can correct the deficiency and prevent permanent skeletal deformities. Thus, the clinical appearance in the image is most consistent with Vitamin D deficiency leading to rickets.

q: An alcoholic patient presented to the outpatient department with ataxia, confusion, and visual disturbances. What is the underlying cause of this condition?
ex: Thiamine Deficiency The classic triad of ataxia (unsteady gait), confusion, and ophthalmoplegia (visual changes/abnormal eye movements) is characteristic of Wernickes encephalopathy. This is an acute neurological emergency caused by a severe deficiency of thiamine (Vitamin B1). Chronic alcoholism is the most common cause in developed countries, as it leads to poor nutrition, impaired thiamine absorption, and increased metabolic demand for the vitamin. If left untreated, Wernickes encephalopathy can progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic condition characterized by profound memory loss and confabulation. The prompt recognition of this triad and immediate administration of high-dose intravenous thiamine is critical to prevent irreversible brain damage. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra (dementia, dermatitis, diarrhea).

q: A patient presented with symptoms suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis, but sputum examination was negative for TB. Chest X-ray findings were consistent with tuberculosis. What should be the next step in management?
ex: CBNAAT The patient is clinically and radiologically suspected of having pulmonary tuberculosis but has a negative sputum smear. This is a common scenario, as sputum smear microscopy has limited sensitivity. The next step according to current diagnostic algorithms is to perform a more sensitive and specific molecular test. The Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (CBNAAT), such as GeneXpert, is the recommended test in this situation. CBNAAT can detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA directly from the sputum sample with much higher sensitivity than microscopy. A major advantage is that it can also simultaneously detect resistance to rifampicin, a key first-line anti-TB drug. Starting treatment based on X-ray alone is not ideal without microbiological confirmation , and simply repeating the same insensitive sputum smear test is less effective than upgrading to a molecular test.

q: A male patient presented with a clean-cut wound and had received tetanus toxoid immunization 10 years ago. What is the appropriate management of this wound?
o: Full course tetanus vaccine to be given
ex: Single dose TT The management of a wound for tetanus prophylaxis depends on the type of wound and the patients vaccination history. This patient has a clean, minor wound. His last tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccine was 10 years ago. According to tetanus prophylaxis guidelines, for a patient with a clean, minor wound whose last dose was 10 or more years ago (or if the history is unknown), a single booster dose of the TT vaccine should be administered. This is sufficient to boost the patients immunity. Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) is not required for clean, minor wounds. A full course is only needed for those with an inadequate primary series. No treatment would be incorrect as immunity wanes over time and a booster is needed after 10 years.

q: A patient has varicella. The management for remaining contacts would be
o: Isolate for 6 days + acyclovir + vzig for 72 hours
Isolate for 14 days + vzig within 48 hours
ex: Isolate for 14 days + vzig within 48 hours The disease referred to here is Varicella (Chickenpox), which is caused by the Varicella-zoster virus. It is a highly contagious disease that spreads through respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicular fluid. When a case of varicella occurs, close contacts—especially those who are susceptible—are at risk of developing the infection. For susceptible contacts, preventive management includes isolation (quarantine) for 14 days, which corresponds to the maximum incubation period of varicella (10–21 days). This helps prevent further spread if the contact becomes infectious. In addition, Varicella Zoster Immune Globulin should be administered within 48 hours of exposure. VZIG provides passive immunity by supplying antibodies against the virus and is particularly recommended for high-risk individuals, such as pregnant women, immuno compromised patients, and newborns exposed to the virus. Other options are incorrect because 6-day isolation applies to infected patients, not contacts, and acyclovir is used mainly for treatment rather than routine prophylaxis of contacts. Therefore, the appropriate management for remaining contacts is isolation for 14 days with VZIG administration within 48 hours of exposure.

q: A premature, low–birth-weight infant was found to have decreased hearing, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and bilateral cataracts. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
ex: Rubella This constellation of birth defects is the classic presentation of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS). This syndrome occurs when a pregnant woman is infected with the rubella virus, especially during the first trimester, and the virus is transmitted to the fetus. The classic triad of CRS consists of: 1) Cataracts (or other eye defects like retinopathy), 2) Sensorineural hearing loss, and 3) Congenital heart defects, with Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary artery stenosis being the most common. In addition to this triad, affected infants often have low birth weight and prematurity. While other congenital infections (part of the TORCH complex) can cause some of these findings, this specific combination, particularly the triad of cataracts, deafness, and PDA, is the hallmark of congenital rubella.

q: A poor farmer with a history of repeated crop failures developed progressive spastic paraparesis, upper motor neuron signs, and gait instability. What is the most likely toxin responsible for this condition?
ex: BOAA This clinical scenario describes neurolathyrism, a crippling neurodegenerative disease. It is caused by the overconsumption of the grass pea, Lathyrus sativus, particularly during times of famine and crop failure when it becomes a staple food. The grass pea contains a neurotoxin called Beta-N-oxalyl-amino-L-alanine (BOAA). This toxin is an excitotoxin that leads to the irreversible degeneration of upper motor neurons. This results in the characteristic clinical picture of a slowly progressive, spastic paraparesis (stiffness and weakness of the legs), hyperreflexia, and an unsteady, scissors-like gait. Aflatoxin is a hepatotoxin and carcinogen. Strychnine causes acute seizures , and ergotoxine causes vasoconstriction (ergotism).

q: Which vitamin is used to treat neurolathyrism
ex: Vit B Neurolathyrism is a neurological condition caused by excessive consumption of the pulse Lathyrus sativus (Kesari dal). This pulse contains a neurotoxin called Beta-oxalyl-L-alpha,beta-diaminopropionic acid, which damages the motor neurons of the spinal cord. Neurolathyrism usually occurs in poor rural populations during drought or famine, when Lathyrus sativus becomes the major dietary component. The disease mainly affects young adults and is characterized by spastic paralysis of the lower limbs, difficulty in walking, exaggerated reflexes, and muscle stiffness, while sensory functions remain normal. Management focuses primarily on prevention and nutritional improvement. Adequate intake of Vitamin B complex is recommended because B-complex vitamins help improve nerve metabolism and neurological function. q: What is the refractive error shown in this image of sturms conoid.
ex: Astigmatism The diagram illustrates the concept of Sturms conoid, which is the optical effect produced by an astigmatic eye. Astigmatism is a refractive error where the eyes refractive surfaces (usually the cornea) are not perfectly spherical. Instead, they have different curvatures in different meridians (e.g., the vertical meridian is steeper than the horizontal). As a result, parallel rays of light entering the eye are not focused to a single point. Instead, they form two separate focal lines at different distances, as shown in the diagram labeled Focus 1 and Focus 2. The pattern of light rays between these two focal lines is known as Sturms conoid. This refractive state is the definition of astigmatism. Myopia and hypermetropia involve a single focal point that is in front of or behind the retina, respectively.

q: A 2-year-old child presented with developmental delay (mental retardation) and was found to have a cherry-red spot on retinal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Tay sach disease The finding of a cherry-red spot on the retina is a classic ophthalmological sign seen in several lysosomal storage diseases. It occurs when lipids or other substances accumulate in the ganglion cells of the retina, making the surrounding macula appear pale or white. This accentuates the normal red color of the underlying choroid at the fovea, which is devoid of ganglion cells. In a child presenting with progressive neurodegeneration (mental retardation) and a cherry-red spot, the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease, which is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A. Niemann-Pick disease (D) can also present with a cherry-red spot, but Tay-Sachs is the classic answer for this combination. Hurler and Hunter syndromes are mucopolysaccharidoses and are not typically associated with this retinal finding.

q: A child presented with swelling of the left eye. What is the most likely diagnosis of this condition?
ex: Dermoid of limbus The image shows a whitish, rounded mass located at the limbus (junction of the cornea and sclera) in a child. This appearance is characteristic of Limbal Dermoid, also called epibulbar dermoid. It is a benign congenital tumor composed of normal tissue in an abnormal location (choristoma) and often contains elements such as hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and connective tissue. Limbal dermoids are usually present since birth or early childhood and most commonly occur at the inferotemporal quadrant of the limbus. Clinically, they appear as a smooth, yellowish-white elevated mass that may partially extend onto the cornea. Large lesions can cause astigmatism, visual disturbance, or cosmetic concerns. q: A patient with a history of dementia was noted to have a golden-yellow ring around the cornea on examination. Which of the following investigations would be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis?
ex: Sr. ceruloplasmin level The combination of neurological symptoms (dementia) and a golden yellow ring around the cornea is pathognomonic for Wilsons disease. The corneal ring is known as a Kayser-Fleischer ring, and it is caused by the deposition of copper in Descemets membrane. Wilsons disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism, leading to toxic accumulation of copper in various organs, primarily the liver and the brain. The diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory investigations that reflect this abnormal copper metabolism. A key diagnostic test is measuring the serum ceruloplasmin level, which is typically low in patients with Wilsons disease because the liver cannot properly incorporate copper into it for secretion. Other tests include 24-hour urinary copper excretion (which is high) and a liver biopsy.

q: A patient with a gradual decrease in vision has recently developed myopia. What is the most likely cause of this refractive condition?
ex: Index myopia The slit lamp image shows nuclear sclerosis, which is the hardening and yellowing of the central part (nucleus) of the crystalline lens. This is a common age-related change and a type of cataract. As the nucleus becomes denser, its refractive index increases. This increase in the refractive power of the lens causes light rays to converge more strongly, shifting the eyes focal point forward. This results in the development or worsening of myopia (nearsightedness). This specific type of myopia, caused by a change in the refractive index of the lens, is known as index myopia. It often leads to a temporary improvement in near vision, sometimes called second sight. Axial myopia is due to a long eyeball, and curvatural myopia is due to a steep cornea.

q: A 10-year-old child presented with tachypnea and severe dehydration. Investigations revealed a random blood glucose level of 550 mg/dL, urine glucose 3+, arterial blood pH of 7.1, and serum bicarbonate of 7 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

q: A child was brought with visible bony deformities, as shown in the image below. Deficiency of which nutrient is responsible for these findings?
ex: Vitamin D The image displays bowed legs (genu varum), a classic skeletal deformity of rickets. Rickets in children is caused by a deficiency of Vitamin D. Vitamin D is crucial for calcium and phosphate homeostasis. It promotes the intestinal absorption of these minerals, which are essential for the proper mineralization of the organic bone matrix (osteoid). In the absence of adequate Vitamin D, the growing bones of a child fail to mineralize, becoming soft and weak. The mechanical stress of weight-bearing then causes the long bones of the legs to bend and bow. Other signs of rickets include widening of the wrists and costochondral junctions (rachitic rosary).

q: Gum bleeding in scurvy is due to
ex: Defect in collagen synthesis Scurvy is the clinical syndrome of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency. Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for the enzymes prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase. These enzymes are responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during the synthesis of collagen, a step that is critical for the formation of stable, cross-linked collagen fibers. A defect in collagen synthesis due to Vitamin C deficiency results in weakened connective tissue throughout the body. This leads to increased fragility of capillary walls, which manifests as the characteristic signs of scurvy, including perifollicular hemorrhage, bruising, and swollen, bleeding gums.
