q: All are true regarding mitochondrial DNA, EXCEPT :
o: All respiratory proteins are synthesized within mitochondria itself
ex: All respiratory proteins are synthesized within mitochondria itself The statement that all respiratory proteins are synthesized within the mitochondria is false. While mitochondria possess their own small, circular, double-stranded genome (mtDNA) and the machinery to transcribe and translate it, this genome is very limited. Human mtDNA encodes only 13 proteins, all of which are essential subunits of the electron transport chain complexes (I, III, IV) and ATP synthase. However, the vast majority of mitochondrial proteins, including the other ~70 subunits of the respiratory chain complexes and all the proteins involved in mtDNA replication, transcription, translation, and metabolism, are encoded by genes in the nuclear DNA. These proteins are synthesized on cytoplasmic ribosomes and then imported into the mitochondria. Therefore, the assembly and function of the respiratory chain require a coordinated effort between both the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. The other statements are true : mtDNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother, and it has a high mutation rate compared to nuclear DNA.

q: Which apolipoprotein is associated with Alzheimer’s disease?
ex: ApoE4 The gene for Apolipoprotein E (APOE) exists in three common alleles : ε2, ε3, and ε4, which code for the ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4 protein isoforms, respectively. While ApoE's primary role is in lipid transport, it is also involved in neuronal repair and amyloid-beta peptide metabolism in the brain. The ApoE4 allele is the single most important and well-established genetic risk factor for the development of late-onset (sporadic) Alzheimer's disease. Individuals who inherit one copy of the ApoE4 allele have approximately a 3-fold increased risk of developing the disease, while those who inherit two copies (homozygotes) have a 10- to 15-fold increased risk and an earlier age of onset. The ApoE4 isoform is thought to contribute to Alzheimer's pathology by impairing the clearance of amyloid-beta from the brain and promoting its aggregation into toxic plaques. In contrast, the ApoE2 allele appears to be protective.

q: Hyperammonaemia inhibits the TCA cycle by depleting :
ex: α-ketoglutarate Hyperammonemia, an excess of ammonia in the blood, is highly toxic to the central nervous system and is the primary cause of hepatic encephalopathy. One of the main mechanisms of ammonia's neurotoxicity is its interference with the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle in brain astrocytes. In the brain, excess ammonia is detoxified by being combined with glutamate to form glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by glutamine synthetase. To replenish the glutamate used in this reaction, another enzyme, glutamate dehydrogenase, combines ammonia with the TCA cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate. In a state of severe hyperammonemia, this reaction is driven strongly in the direction of glutamate synthesis, which effectively depletes the brain's pool of α-ketoglutarate. The loss of this critical TCA cycle intermediate impairs the cycle's function, leading to a deficit in cellular energy (ATP) production and contributing significantly to the neurological dysfunction seen in hepatic encephalopathy.

q: Which Amino acid is used to synthesize Nitric oxide :
ex: Arginine Nitric oxide (NO) is a vital gaseous signaling molecule with roles in vasodilation, neurotransmission, and immunity. It is synthesized endogenously from the amino acid L-arginine. This conversion is catalyzed by a family of enzymes known as nitric oxide synthases (NOS). The NOS enzyme utilizes the guanidinium group of L-arginine as the source for the nitrogen atom in nitric oxide. In the process, L-arginine is oxidized to produce nitric oxide and L-citrulline as a co-product. This enzymatic reaction requires several cofactors, including molecular oxygen, NADPH, and tetrahydrobiopterin. The availability of the substrate, L-arginine, can be a rate-limiting factor for NO production in certain physiological and pathological states. The other amino acids listed are precursors for different molecules; for example, tyrosine is the precursor for catecholamines.

q: Menkes disease is caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?
ex: Lysyl oxidase Menkes disease is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder of copper metabolism. It is caused by a mutation in the ATP7A gene, which codes for a copper-transporting ATPase. This defect leads to impaired absorption of copper from the diet and a failure to transport copper out of cells and into the bloodstream. The resulting systemic copper deficiency leads to the dysfunction of numerous copper-dependent enzymes. One of the most critically affected enzymes is lysyl oxidase. This enzyme is essential for the final step in the synthesis of collagen and elastin; it catalyzes the cross-linking of collagen and elastin fibers, which gives connective tissues their strength and elasticity. The deficiency of lysyl oxidase in Menkes disease leads to defective connective tissue, resulting in many of the characteristic clinical features, such as tortuous arteries, skin laxity, and brittle, kinky hair. NODIA 556=== page 544 Examination Paper 2019 (A) Projection fibres (B) Short association fibres (C) Long association fibres (D) Commissural fibres Ans : (A) Projection fibres The image shows a coronal section of the brain with the internal capsule highlighted. The internal capsule is a massive, compact bundle of white matter fibers. These fibers are classified as projection fibers. Projection fibers are axons that connect the cerebral cortex with subcortical structures, the brainstem, and the spinal cord. They project information to and from the cortex. The internal capsule contains both ascending (thalamocortical) and descending (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine) tracts. In contrast, commissural fibers (D) are fibers that connect corresponding areas of the two cerebral hemispheres (e.g., the corpus callosum). Association fibers (B, C) connect different areas within the same cerebral hemisphere. Because the internal capsule is the primary conduit for fibers ascending to and descending from the cerebral cortex, it is composed of projection fibers.

q: Which anatomical structure is indicated by the arrow in the image?
ex: Fornix The CT scan of the brain shown in the image indicates a midline structure located near the lateral ventricles, highlighted by the red arrow. This structure corresponds to the fornix, an important component of the limbic system. The fornix is a C-shaped bundle of white matter fibers that serves as a major output tract of the hippocampus. Anatomically, the fornix lies just beneath the corpus callosum and above the thalamus, forming part of the roof of the third ventricle and the medial walls of the lateral ventricles. It connects the hippocampus to other limbic structures such as the mammillary bodies and septal nuclei, playing a key role in memory processing and emotional regulation. The other options represent different structures. The great vein of Galen is a deep cerebral vein located more posteriorly. The pineal gland lies posterior to the third ventricle in the midline. The falx cerebri is a dural fold separating the two cerebral hemispheres and appears along the midline of the skull. Thus, the structure indicated by the arrow is the fornix.

q: Which nerve innervates the structure indicated in the image?
ex: Median nerve The image displays the intrinsic muscles of the hand, with an arrow pointing to the lumbrical muscles. The lumbricals are four small muscles that originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and insert into the extensor expansions of the digits. Their action is to flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints while extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. The innervation of the lumbricals is unique and is divided between the median and ulnar nerves. The first and second lumbricals (the radial two, for the index and middle fingers) are innervated by the median nerve. The third and fourth lumbricals (the ulnar two, for the ring and little fingers) are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Since the arrow appears to point towards the more radial lumbricals, the median nerve is the correct answer.

q: Identify the marked structure in the image.
ex: Cerebellum The image provided is a sagittal view of the human brain, showing its major components. The arrow is pointing to the large structure located in the posterior cranial fossa, inferior to the cerebrum and posterior to the pons and medulla of the brainstem. This is the cerebellum. The cerebellum is a highly convoluted structure with a characteristic, finely foliated appearance, which is evident in the image. It is a crucial part of the motor system and plays a vital role in coordinating voluntary movements, posture, balance, and motor learning. It is connected to the brainstem via three large white matter tracts : the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles. The cerebrum (A) is the largest part of the brain superiorly, and the corpus callosum (C) is the white matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.

q: The nerve injured in Frey's syndrome is :
ex: Auriculotemporal Nerve Frey's syndrome, also known as gustatory sweating, is a condition characterized by sweating and flushing of the skin in the preauricular and temporal region (the area supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve) that is triggered by eating or thinking about food. It is a common complication of surgery involving the parotid gland, such as a parotidectomy. The syndrome is caused by an injury to the auriculotemporal nerve during the surgery. This nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland to stimulate salivation. After being injured, these parasympathetic fibers undergo aberrant regeneration. Instead of reinnervating the parotid gland, they mistakenly reinnervate the sympathetic sweat glands and blood vessels in the overlying skin. As a result, when the patient eats, the gustatory stimulus intended to produce saliva instead activates these misdirected fibers, causing localized sweating and flushing.

q: Upward movement of the thyroid gland is prevented by which of the following structures?
ex: Sternothyroid muscle The thyroid gland is intimately connected to the larynx by the suspensory ligament of Berry and is enclosed within the pretracheal fascia, which also attaches to the larynx. These connections cause the thyroid to move superiorly and inferiorly during swallowing. However, excessive upward movement is restrained by the infrahyoid muscles, commonly known as the strap muscles. The sternothyroid muscle, in particular, plays a crucial role in this restraint. Originating from the posterior surface of the manubrium sterni and inserting onto the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, this muscle lies directly anterior to the thyroid gland. Its primary action is to depress the larynx after it has been elevated during swallowing or phonation. By anchoring the larynx (and thus the attached thyroid) to the sternum, the sternothyroid muscle acts as a tether, physically preventing significant superior displacement of the thyroid gland. The other structures listed either facilitate its movement with the larynx (Berry's ligament, pretracheal fascia) or are located superior to it (thyrohyoid membrane).

q: The elongated path of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is a result of the persistence of which embryonic aortic arch?
ex: 6th Arch The asymmetrical course of the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves is a direct consequence of the embryological development of the aortic arches. Both nerves initially hook around the 6th aortic arch on their respective sides. On the right side, the distal portion of the 6th arch and the entire 5th arch artery degenerate. This allows the right recurrent laryngeal nerve to ascend and hook underneath the next persistent structure, which is the 4th aortic arch artery (forming the right subclavian artery). On the left side, however, the distal part of the 6th aortic arch persists to form the ductus arteriosus (which later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum). Because this structure remains, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is trapped and cannot ascend. It is held down in the thorax, where it loops under the arch of the aorta (formed by the left 4th arch) adjacent to the ligamentum arteriosum. This explains its longer, recurrent course from the chest back up to the larynx.

q: Ligation of the hepatic artery will compromise blood flow to which of the following arteries?
o: Right gastric and Right gastroepiploic artery
Right gastric and Left gastric artery
Right gastroepiploic and Short gastric vessels
Right gastric and Short gastric vessels
ex: Right gastric and Right gastroepiploic artery The common hepatic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk. It gives rise to the gastroduodenal artery before continuing as the hepatic artery proper. Ligation of the common hepatic artery proximal to this branch would compromise all of its downstream vessels. The gastroduodenal artery gives rise to the right gastroepiploic artery, which supplies the greater curvature of the stomach. The hepatic artery proper gives rise to the right gastric artery, which supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach. Therefore, ligating the common hepatic artery would directly impair blood flow to both the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries. The left gastric artery (B) is a direct branch of the celiac trunk and would not be affected. The short gastric vessels (C, D) are branches of the splenic artery, which is another direct branch of the celiac trunk, so their supply would also be preserved. The dual supply to the stomach from other celiac branches often provides sufficient collateral circulation.

q: Which of the following structures in females is a remnant of the Wolffian duct?
ex: Gartner's cyst In embryonic development, males and females initially have both Wolffian (mesonephric) and Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts. In females, the absence of testosterone causes the Wolffian ducts to degenerate, while the Müllerian ducts develop into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. However, remnants of the Wolffian duct can sometimes persist in females. These vestigial structures are known as Gartner's ducts and are typically found in the broad ligament or along the lateral walls of the cervix and vagina. If these ducts accumulate fluid, they can form a benign, fluid-filled sac known as a Gartner's cyst. These cysts are the most common remnant of the Wolffian duct system in females. The Pouch of Douglas (A) and the uterovesical pouch (B) are peritoneal reflections. The broad ligament (D) is a peritoneal fold that supports the female reproductive organs.

q: Which of the following nerves does not contribute to the innervation of the extraocular muscles?
ex: Ophthalmic nerve The motor innervation to the six extraocular muscles is provided by three specific cranial nerves. This is commonly remembered by the mnemonic (LR6SO4)3. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) supplies the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies only the superior oblique muscle. The abducent nerve (CN VI) supplies only the lateral rectus muscle. The ophthalmic nerve, which is the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), is a purely sensory nerve. It is not involved in motor supply to the extraocular muscles. Instead, it provides sensation to the eyeball, cornea, conjunctiva, upper eyelid, forehead, and scalp. Therefore, the ophthalmic nerve is not part of the motor nerve supply to the muscles that move the eye.

q: Claudication resulting from popliteal-femoral incompetence primarily affects which area?
ex: Calf Claudication refers to muscle pain or cramping that is induced by exercise and relieved by rest. It is a hallmark symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD), caused by insufficient blood flow to meet the metabolic demands of the exercising muscle. The location of the claudication pain directly corresponds to the muscle group distal to the arterial stenosis or occlusion. The femoropopliteal arterial segment, comprising the superficial femoral artery and the popliteal artery, is the most common site of atherosclerotic disease in the lower limbs. When this segment is incompetent (stenosed), blood flow is restricted to the muscles of the lower leg. The calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) have a very high oxygen demand during walking. Therefore, stenosis in the femoral or popliteal arteries most classically and primarily causes claudication pain in the calf. q: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of blood in the stools. Examination reveals a polypoid mass in the rectum, and biopsy findings are shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
ex: Juvenile polyp The presentation of painless rectal bleeding in a young child with a rectal polyp is classic for a juvenile polyp. These are the most common type of colon polyp found in children. Histologically, juvenile polyps are a type of hamartoma, not a true neoplasm. The biopsy image would show the characteristic features : the polyp is composed of an abundance of inflamed lamina propria containing numerous large, cystically dilated glands that are filled with mucin. The surface of the polyp is often eroded, which accounts for the bleeding. These polyps are benign and have virtually no malignant potential when they occur sporadically. This is in contrast to adenomatous polyps (A, D), which are pre-malignant and are characterized by glandular dysplasia, and are very rare in this age group.

q: A 30-year-old woman reports easy fatigability, exertional breathlessness, weight loss, and frequent falls. Examination shows reduced vibration sense bilaterally, and her hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL. After folate therapy, her anemia improved but her neurological symptoms became worse. What is the most likely explanation for this outcome?
o: Deficiency of folate reductase in CNS.
Folate therapy caused rapid use of Vitamin B12 stores, aggravating symptoms
ex: Folate therapy caused rapid use of Vitamin B12 stores, aggravating symptoms This patient presents with both macrocytic anemia (suggested by the symptoms) and neurological symptoms (decreased vibration sense, falls), which is highly indicative of Vitamin B12 deficiency. A deficiency of either B12 or folate can cause megaloblastic anemia. However, only B12 deficiency causes the neurological demyelination that leads to subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. If a patient with an underlying B12 deficiency is treated with folic acid alone, the folate can partially correct the anemia by providing substrate for DNA synthesis. This is known as a hematological remission. However, this correction consumes the remaining small stores of functional Vitamin B12 for hematopoiesis. This steals the B12 away from the nervous system, thereby accelerating the progression of the irreversible neurological damage. This phenomenon of worsening neurological symptoms after folate administration is a classic pitfall in the management of megaloblastic anemia.

q: A 45-year-old chronic smoker presents with cough. A biopsy is performed, and the histology is shown in the image. Which type of cellular change has taken place in this patient?
ex: Metaplasia The image depicts a change in the lining of a bronchus. The normal respiratory epithelium, which is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, is on the left. On the right, this has been replaced by a more rugged, stratified squamous epithelium. This reversible change of one differentiated cell type to another is known as metaplasia. In chronic smokers, the constant irritation from the smoke causes the delicate ciliated columnar cells of the bronchial lining to be replaced by the more robust stratified squamous cells, which are better able to withstand the chemical insult. While this squamous metaplasia is initially a protective adaptation, it is not a normal state. The new epithelium lacks cilia and mucus-secreting goblet cells, impairing the mucociliary clearance mechanism. Importantly, this metaplastic tissue is fertile ground for the future development of dysplasia and, eventually, squamous cell carcinoma if the irritation continues.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with thyroid swelling, has elevated TSH levels, and postoperative pathology shows lymphocytic infiltration along with Hurthle cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Hashimoto's thyroiditis This combination of clinical and pathological findings is classic for Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is an autoimmune disease where the thyroid gland is progressively destroyed. The elevated TSH level indicates that the pituitary gland is trying to stimulate a failing thyroid gland (primary hypothyroidism). The goiter (thyroid swelling) is due to the inflammatory infiltrate and compensatory hyperplasia. The definitive diagnosis comes from the histology, which is characterized by two key features : a dense, diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid parenchyma, often with the formation of germinal centers, and the presence of Hürthle cells (or Askanazy cells). Hürthle cells are large, eosinophilic thyroid follicular cells that have undergone metaplastic change in response to the chronic inflammation. Graves' disease (A) causes hyperthyroidism with low TSH.

q: Which characteristic finding will appear on a cardiac biopsy from a patient who has sustained reperfusion injury following a myocardial infarction?
ex: Eosinophilic contraction bands Reperfusion injury is a paradoxical phenomenon where tissue damage is exacerbated after blood flow is restored to an area that was previously ischemic. In the context of a myocardial infarction, when a coronary artery is reopened (e.g., by angioplasty or thrombolysis), the sudden influx of oxygen and calcium into the severely damaged cardiomyocytes leads to a specific type of necrosis called contraction band necrosis. This is characterized histologically by the formation of eosinophilic contraction bands. These are intensely pink (eosinophilic), transverse bands within the cytoplasm of the myocytes. They represent hypercontracted and ruptured sarcomeres, caused by the massive calcium influx into the cells that have damaged cell membranes. This finding is a hallmark of an MI that has been reperfused and is distinct from the coagulative necrosis seen in non-reperfused infarcts.

q: Loss of foot processes is classically seen in which condition?

q: What is the main characteristic of chemotaxis in white blood cells?

Various substances, known as chemoattractants (e.g., bacterial products, complement components like C5a, and chemokines like IL-8), are released at the site of inflammation. Leukocytes have receptors for these substances, allowing them to sense the concentration gradient. They then actively move from an area of lower concentration towards the area of higher concentration, directing them precisely to the source of the inflammatory stimulus. q: Which of the following is not a prokinetic agent?

q: Which antihypertensive medication should be avoided in patients who have elevated serum uric acid levels?

However, a well-known metabolic side effect is hyperuricemia (an increase in serum uric acid levels). Thiazides increase uric acid levels by competing with urate for secretion at the organic acid transporter in the proximal renal tubules. This reduced renal excretion leads to an accumulation of uric acid in the blood. In susceptible individuals, this can precipitate an acute attack of gout. Therefore, thiazide diuretics should be avoided or used with caution in patients with a history of gout or pre-existing hyperuricemia. In contrast, some other antihypertensives, such as the ARB losartan, have a mild uricosuric effect and can actually lower uric acid levels, making them a better choice in these patients. q: What is the mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to penicillins through beta- lactamase production?

These enzymes confer resistance by directly inactivating the antibiotic. The beta-lactam ring is the core chemical structure of all penicillin-class antibiotics and is essential for their antibacterial activity. Beta-lactamase enzymes are hydrolases that specifically target and cleave the amide bond within this beta-lactam ring. This enzymatic cleavage breaks the drug's structure, opening the ring and rendering the antibiotic molecule completely inactive and unable to bind to its target, the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) in the bacterial cell wall. Altered PBPs (A) is another important resistance mechanism (seen in MRSA), but it is distinct from the action of beta-lactamase. q: A patient receiving lithium therapy develops hypertension and is started on a thiazide diuretic. After a few days, signs of lithium toxicity such as coarse tremors appear. What is the most likely mechanism behind this drug interaction?

q: Which of the following hormones acts via a tyrosine kinase receptor?

The phosphorylated receptor then acts as a docking site and phosphorylates other intracellular substrate proteins, such as Insulin Receptor Substrate (IRS). This initiates a complex downstream signaling cascade that ultimately mediates the diverse metabolic effects of insulin, such as glucose uptake into cells. In contrast, TSH, LH, and MSH are all peptide hormones that bind to G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), which exert their effects through second messenger systems like cyclic AMP, not through a tyrosine kinase receptor.

q: Zero-order (saturation) kinetics is independent of which of the following factors?
ex: Plasma concentration Drug elimination can follow either first-order or zero-order kinetics. In zero-order kinetics, the rate of elimination is constant and is independent of the drug's plasma concentration. This occurs when the metabolic or elimination pathways are saturated. A constant amount of the drug is eliminated per unit of time, regardless of how much drug is in the body. Classic examples include ethanol, phenytoin, and aspirin at high doses. In contrast, in first-order kinetics (which most drugs follow at therapeutic doses), a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit of time, and the rate of elimination is directly proportional to the plasma concentration. In zero-order kinetics, concepts like a constant half-life and clearance are no longer valid, as they change with the plasma concentration.

q: Identify the phenomena in the image.
ex: Putrefaction The image displays a human body in an advanced state of decomposition. The key features visible are extensive skin slippage (desquamation), discoloration, and bloating. This entire process is known as putrefaction. Putrefaction is the destruction of the soft tissues of the body by the action of anaerobic microorganisms, primarily bacteria and fungi originating from the gastrointestinal tract. These bacteria proliferate after death, breaking down tissues and producing various gases (like hydrogen sulfide and methane). This gas production leads to bloating of the body, and the breakdown of hemoglobin creates pigments like sulphemoglobin, which causes a greenish-black discoloration. The breakdown of the junction between the epidermis and dermis leads to the formation of putrefactive blisters and eventually causes the skin to slip off. These findings are characteristic of postmortem decomposition and are distinct from the changes seen in burns or scalds. NODIA 459=== Ans : (A) Sulphur dioxide, smoke, and particulate matter Routine monitoring of ambient air pollution focuses on a set of key criteria pollutants that are known to be widespread and have significant health effects. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in many countries, including India's National Air Quality Index, is based on the measurement of several pollutants. The most fundamental and historically important indicators used for routine monitoring are sulfur dioxide (SO2), smoke, and suspended particulate matter (SPM), particularly PM2.5 and PM10. SO2 is a primary indicator of pollution from burning fossil fuels like coal. Smoke and particulate matter are products of combustion and have profound respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts. While other pollutants like carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, ozone, and lead are also important and are included in comprehensive AQI calculations, the combination of SO2, smoke, and particulate matter represents the core group of pollutants that have traditionally formed the basis of air pollution monitoring.

q: Which statistical measure is used to compare the variation between two different data sets?
ex: Coefficient of variation When comparing the variability or dispersion of two different datasets, especially when their means are significantly different or they are measured in different units, using the standard deviation or variance directly can be misleading. The coefficient of variation (CV) is the appropriate statistical measure for this purpose. The CV is a standardized, unitless measure of relative variability. It is calculated by dividing the standard deviation (σ) by the mean (μ) and is often expressed as a percentage : CV = (σ / μ) × 100%. By expressing the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, the CV allows for a direct comparison of the degree of variation between two or more groups, independent of their respective means or units of measurement. A higher CV indicates greater relative variability.

q: In which type of management or evaluation method is the benefit expressed in natural units?
ex: Cost-effective analysis Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is a type of economic evaluation used to compare the relative costs and outcomes of two or more different interventions. A key feature of CEA is that the health outcomes, or benefits, are measured in natural units. These are non-monetary units that are directly relevant to the health condition being studied. Examples of natural units include lives saved, cases of disease prevented, years of life gained, or a clinical measurement like reduction in blood pressure (mmHg). The result of a CEA is typically expressed as a ratio, such as the cost per life saved. This contrasts with cost-benefit analysis (CBA), where both the costs and the health benefits are converted into monetary values, which can be ethically and methodologically challenging.

q: The difference in incidence rates between the exposed and non-exposed groups is best expressed by which measure?
ex: Attributable Risk Attributable Risk (AR), also known as Risk Difference or Excess Risk, is an absolute measure of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is calculated as the difference between the incidence rate of the disease in the exposed group and the incidence rate in the unexposed group (AR = Ie - Iu). The Attributable Risk represents the excess risk of disease in the exposed group that is directly attributable to the exposure itself. It answers the question : How much of the disease in exposed individuals is due to the exposure? This measure is particularly useful from a public health perspective as it indicates the potential reduction in disease incidence that could be achieved if the exposure were eliminated from the exposed group. Relative Risk, in contrast, is a ratio (Ie / Iu) and measures the strength of the association.

q: If the value of one variable is known, which coefficient can be used to estimate or determine the other variable?
ex: Coefficient of Regression A regression analysis is a statistical method used to model the relationship between a dependent variable (the one you want to predict) and one or more independent variables (the ones you use to make the prediction). The output of a simple linear regression is an equation of the form Y = a + bX, where 'Y' is the dependent variable, 'X' is the independent variable, 'a' is the intercept, and 'b' is the regression coefficient. The regression coefficient ('b') quantifies the change in the dependent variable 'Y' for every one-unit change in the independent variable 'X'. Therefore, if you are given the value of one variable (X) and you know the regression equation (including the coefficient), you can use it to predict or find the corresponding value of the other variable (Y). The correlation coefficient (B) only measures the strength and direction of the relationship, it does not allow for prediction.

q: In which of the following situations is prospective screening usually carried out?
o: Diabetes mellitus screening for a 40-year- old male
ex: Neonate for thyroid diseases Prospective screening refers to the proactive screening of a defined population, often at a specific time point, to detect disease early, usually before the onset of symptoms. Newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism is a quintessential example of universal prospective screening. This is a public health program where every single newborn is screened via a heel-prick blood test within the first few days of life. The aim is to prospectively identify all affected infants to initiate thyroid hormone replacement therapy immediately, thereby preventing the severe and irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism) associated with the untreated condition. While screening immigrants (B) is also prospective, newborn screening is a more universal and classic example. Pap smears (C) and diabetes screening (D) are often performed opportunistically when a person visits a healthcare provider for another reason, although they can also be part of prospective programs.

q: A researcher aims to establish an association between smoking and COPD by using hospital patient records and cigarette sales data from government sources. Which type of study design does this represent?
ex: Ecological study This study design is an ecological study. The defining feature of an ecological study is that the unit of analysis is a population or group, not an individual. In this scenario, the researcher is not linking an individual's smoking habit to their personal risk of COPD. Instead, they are correlating aggregate-level data : the prevalence or incidence of COPD in a population (from hospital records) with the per capita cigarette sales in that same population (from government data). The researcher is looking for an association between the exposure and the outcome at the population level. A major limitation of this study design is the ecological fallacy, which is the risk of making an incorrect inference about individuals based on the aggregate data of the group to which they belong.

q: A study assessing malnutrition selected 100 children each from rural and urban areas. Thirty rural children and twenty urban children were found to be malnourished. Which statistical test is appropriate to compare these two groups?
o: The standard error of the mean
ex: Chi-square This study aims to compare the proportion of malnourished children between two independent groups (rural vs. urban). The data collected are categorical (malnourished or not malnourished). The appropriate statistical test to determine if there is a significant association between two categorical variables is the chi-square (χ²) test of independence. This test compares the observed frequencies in each category (e.g., 30 rural malnourished, 70 rural not-malnourished, etc.) with the frequencies that would be expected if there were no association between the area of residence and nutritional status. A significant chi-square statistic would indicate that the prevalence of malnutrition is different between the rural and urban groups. A t-test (A) is used to compare means of continuous data, and ANOVA (D) is used to compare the means of more than two groups.

q: The disinfectant action of bleaching powder is primarily due to which component?
ex: Hypochlorous acid Bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is a common disinfectant, especially for water purification. When bleaching powder is dissolved in water, it hydrolyzes to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and calcium hydroxide. It is the hypochlorous acid that is the primary active disinfecting agent. Hypochlorous acid is a powerful oxidizing agent that effectively kills microorganisms by destroying their essential enzymes and structural proteins. The amount of free available chlorine, which exists primarily as hypochlorous acid and the hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻) in equilibrium, determines the disinfecting power. HOCl is a much more potent disinfectant than the OCl⁻ ion. Although the process releases chlorine, it is the resulting hypochlorous acid in the aqueous solution that carries out the main bactericidal action. Chloramines (D) are formed when chlorine reacts with ammonia.

q: Which of the following antibodies is not transferred from the mother to the fetus?
ex: Polio During pregnancy, certain maternal antibodies are transferred from mother to fetus through the placenta. This transfer mainly involves IgG, which provides passive immunity to the newborn during the first few months of life. Antibodies against diseases such as Diphtheria, Pertussis, and Tetanus are mainly of the IgG type and are effectively transferred across the placenta. This is why maternal vaccination during pregnancy (such as the Tdap vaccine) can protect the newborn against these infections. However, immunity against Poliomyelitis is primarily mediated by secretory IgA antibodies, especially when immunity comes from the oral polio vaccine. IgA antibodies do not cross the placenta, so they are not significantly transferred from mother to fetus. Therefore, antibodies against polio are generally not transferred effectively to the fetus, making (A) Polio the correct answer.

q: Under the Mental Healthcare Act (MHA) 2017, what is the maximum duration for which a person can be admitted voluntarily?
ex: 30 days The Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA) of 2017 outlines the procedures for admission to a mental health establishment. For a minor who is admitted with the consent of their nominated representative, the Act specifies the duration for which they can be admitted. Section 87 of the Act states that a medical officer or psychiatrist who has examined the minor can recommend their admission. However, this admission is for a limited period. The Act clarifies that no minor shall be admitted as an independent patient for a period exceeding thirty days at a time. If further stay is required, a reassessment must be conducted. This provision is designed to safeguard the rights of the minor and ensure that institutionalization is regularly reviewed and justified, preventing indefinite stays without proper oversight.

q: Blood bags should be discarded in which color- coded biomedical waste disposal bag?
ex: Yellow bag According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules in India, different categories of waste are segregated into specific color-coded bags or containers to ensure safe handling and disposal. Blood bags fall under the Yellow category. This category is designated for human anatomical waste, animal anatomical waste, soiled waste (items contaminated with blood and body fluids), expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste, and microbiology & biotechnology waste. Specifically, items like blood bags that have contained human blood are considered highly infectious soiled waste. They must be placed in the yellow-coded, non-chlorinated plastic bags and sent for incineration or plasma pyrolysis to ensure complete and safe destruction of any potential blood-borne pathogens. The black bag is for general municipal waste, the red for recyclable plastics, and the white for sharps.

q: Which of the following conditions is not considered an absolute contraindication to the use of an intrauterine device (IUD)?
ex: Uterine malformation The World Health Organization (WHO) provides Medical Eligibility Criteria for contraceptive use. For Intrauterine Devices (IUDs), there are several absolute contra indications (Category 4), where the risk is unacceptable. These include suspected or confirmed pregnancy, current pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or a high risk of STIs, and unexplained or undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, as this could be a sign of an underlying malignancy. A uterine malformation (such as a bicornuate or septate uterus) that significantly distorts the uterine cavity is also a contraindication. However, this is often considered a relative contraindication (Category 3 or 4 depending on severity), as the IUD may not fit properly, leading to a higher risk of expulsion or perforation. Compared to active pregnancy or PID, which are absolute contra indications, a uterine anomaly's contraindication can be more nuanced, making it the most likely answer for not an absolute contraindication in all cases. q: Identify the organism shown in the image.
ex: Trichuris trichiura The image displays the characteristic eggs of the nematode Trichuris trichiura, commonly known as the whipworm. These eggs have a highly distinctive and pathognomonic appearance, making them easily identifiable on microscopic examination of a stool sample. The eggs are barrel-shaped or lemon-shaped and have a thick, smooth, bile-stained (yellowish-brown) shell. At either end of the egg, there is a prominent, translucent polar plug, which gives the egg its characteristic appearance. The presence of these unique barrel-shaped eggs with polar plugs in a stool sample is diagnostic for trichuriasis, an infection caused by the whipworm. The eggs of the other parasites listed have entirely different morphologies : Ancylostoma eggs are oval with a thin shell, Paragonimus eggs are operculated, and Strongyloides is typically diagnosed by finding larvae, not eggs, in the stool.

q: Which culture media is used for E. coli 0157?
ex: SMAC Escherichia coli O157 :H7 is a significant serotype of enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) that causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome. Most strains of E. coli are able to ferment the sugar sorbitol. However, E. coli O157 :H7 is unusual in that it is a non-sorbitol fermenter. This biochemical characteristic is exploited for its selective isolation in the laboratory. The specific culture medium used is Sorbitol MacConkey Agar (SMAC). This medium is a modification of MacConkey agar where lactose is replaced with sorbitol. On SMAC agar, typical sorbitol-fermenting E. coli strains will produce pink or red colonies. In contrast, the non-sorbitol fermenting E. coli O157 :H7 will produce colorless or neutral-colored colonies, allowing for their presumptive identification and selection for further testing.

q: Donovanosis is caused by which organism?
ex: K. granulomatis Donovanosis, also known as granuloma inguinale, is a chronic, progressive ulcerative sexually transmitted infection. The causative agent is Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly known as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). This is a Gram-negative intracellular bacterium. The diagnosis is typically made by microscopic examination of a crush preparation or biopsy from the lesion, stained with Giemsa or Wright stain. The pathognomonic finding is the presence of Donovan bodies, which are clusters of the small, encapsulated bacterial coccobacilli seen within the cytoplasm of large mononuclear cells (macrophages). The disease presents as painless, beefy-red, friable ulcers that progressively expand. H. ducreyi (A) causes chancroid, L. donovani (B) causes leishmaniasis, and T. pallidum (D) causes syphilis.

q: The immunoglobulin structure illustrated in the image corresponds to which class of antibody?
ex: IgA The image displays a diagram of a dimeric immunoglobulin. It shows two individual Y-shaped antibody monomers linked together by a small protein called the J chain. The structure also includes another protein wrapped around the Fc portions, which is the secretory component. This specific dimeric structure, containing a J chain and a secretory component, is the characteristic form of secretory IgA. While IgA exists as a monomer in the serum, it is secreted onto mucosal surfaces (in tears, saliva, breast milk, and gastrointestinal/respiratory secretions) as this stable dimeric form. The secretory component protects the antibody from degradation by proteolytic enzymes in the harsh mucosal environment. IgM (C) exists as a pentamer, also joined by a J chain, but has five monomers. IgG (B) and IgE (D) exist only as monomers.

q: Which fungal infection is transmitted through traumatic implantation into the skin?
ex: Sporothrix Sporotrichosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, is the classic example of a fungal infection acquired via traumatic inoculation. This fungus lives in soil, sphagnum moss, and on plants. The infection typically occurs when the contaminated plant material (like a rose thorn, hence the name rose gardener's disease) causes a small cut or puncture wound in the skin, directly inoculating the fungus into the subcutaneous tissue. This results in the formation of a small, painless nodule at the site of inoculation, which may ulcerate. The infection then classically spreads along the lymphatic channels, forming a chain of secondary nodules and ulcers known as lymphogenous sporotrichosis. In contrast, the other fungi listed (Blastomycosis, Coccidioidomycosis, and Para coccidioidomycosis) are systemic mycoses that are primarily acquired by inhalation of airborne spores into the lungs.

q: A patient presents with one-sided proptosis along with bilateral sixth cranial (abducent) nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Cavernous sinus thrombosis This combination of signs is highly suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST). The cavernous sinuses are paired venous structures located on either side of the sella turcica, which contain several critical cranial nerves (III, IV, V1, V2, and VI) and the internal carotid artery. The abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) has a unique intra cavernous course, running freely within the sinus, making it particularly vulnerable to any process that increases pressure within the sinus. Because the two cavernous sinuses have intercommunicating channels, a unilateral process like a septic thrombosis can quickly lead to bilateral signs. Therefore, the presentation of unilateral proptosis (due to venous congestion) combined with a bilateral abducens nerve palsy (due to elevated pressure affecting the nerves on both sides) is a classic finding in CST. Orbital cellulitis typically causes unilateral signs.

q: What is the characteristic finding of fungal ulcers?
ex: Satellite lesions Fungal keratitis (a fungal corneal ulcer) has several clinical features that help to distinguish it from bacterial ulcers. One of the most characteristic findings is the presence of satellite lesions. The main ulcer typically has a feathery, indistinct border and a dry, raised appearance. In addition to this central infiltrate, smaller, discrete foci of inflammation can be seen in the surrounding stroma, separate from the primary lesion. These are the satellite lesions, and their presence is highly suggestive of a filamentous fungal infection (like Aspergillus or Fusarium), as the hyphae can grow and proliferate through the corneal stroma to create these separate foci. A thick, white hypopyon (D) and an endothelial plaque are also common. A dendritic ulcer (B) is pathognomonic for herpes simplex keratitis.

q: Which drug, used in patients with raised intraocular pressure and optic disc changes, acts by increasing uveoscleral outflow?
ex: Latanoprost The management of glaucoma (characterized by increased IOP and optic disc changes) involves lowering the IOP. This can be achieved by either decreasing the production of aqueous humor or increasing its outflow from the eye. There are two main outflow pathways : the conventional trabecular meshwork pathway and the unconventional uveoscleral pathway. Prostaglandin analogs, such as Latanoprost, are a first-line class of medications for glaucoma that work primarily by increasing the outflow of aqueous humor through the uveoscleral pathway. They do this by relaxing the ciliary muscle and remodeling the extracellular matrix in the uveoscleral space, which reduces resistance to outflow. Pilocarpine (B) increases outflow through the trabecular meshwork. Timolol (D, a beta-blocker) and dorzolamide (C, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) work by decreasing the production of aqueous humor.

q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has been receiving long-term treatment and develops blurred vision after two years. Examination reveals corneal opacity. Which drug is most likely responsible for this finding?
ex: Chloroquine Several medications used to treat rheumatoid arthritis can have ocular side effects. One of the most well-known toxicities is associated with the antimalarial drugs chloroquine and hydroxy chloroquine. While the most feared complication is an irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy, these drugs can also affect the cornea. A characteristic finding is cornea verticillata (also known as vortex keratopathy), which is the deposition of the drug in the corneal epithelium. This creates fine, greyish or golden-brown opacities that swirl outwards from a point below the pupil in a whorl-like pattern. While often asymptomatic, these corneal opacities can sometimes cause blurred vision, glare, and halos around lights. The development of corneal opacities in a patient on long-term treatment for RA is highly suggestive of chloroquine or hydroxy chloroquine keratoplasty.

q: Which of the following statements correctly describes Nutcracker esophagus?
o: There is extremely forceful peristaltic activity leading to episodes of chest pain and dysphagia.
There is no medical treatment available.
It is a type of esophageal malignancy.
ex: There is extremely forceful peristaltic activity leading to episodes of chest pain and dysphagia. Nutcracker esophagus, also known as hypertensive peristalsis, is a motility disorder of the esophagus. It is defined by manometric findings of normal, coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body, but with extremely high-amplitude or long-duration contractions. The peristaltic waves are normally sequenced but are simply too powerful. This hyper contractility is thought to be the cause of the primary symptoms, which are non-cardiac chest pain and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). The diagnosis is made exclusively by high-resolution esophageal manometry, which will show distal contractile integral (DCI) values greater than 8,000 mmHg·s·cm. It is a benign motility disorder, not a malignancy (C is incorrect). Medical treatments, though often of limited efficacy, are available and include calcium channel blockers, nitrates, and proton pump inhibitors (B is incorrect).

q: Which prognostic scoring system for liver disease is depicted in the image?
ex: Child-Pugh score While no picture is provided, the question asks for a prognostic scoring system for liver conditions. The Child-Pugh score (also known as the Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) is a widely used system to assess the severity and prognosis of chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It was originally designed to predict mortality during surgery but is now used to predict overall prognosis and the need for liver transplantation. The score is calculated based on five clinical and laboratory parameters : serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time (or INR), and the degree of ascites and hepatic encephalopathy. Patients are classified into three classes (A, B, or C) based on their total score, with Class A having the best prognosis and Class C having the worst. The MELD score is also used, especially for transplant allocation, but Child-Pugh is a classic prognostic tool.

q: A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent infections and a characteristic skin rash, as shown in the image. Laboratory investigations reveal thrombocytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome The clinical triad of recurrent infections, eczema (the rash shown), and thrombocytopenia in a male child is the classic presentation of Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS). WAS is a rare, X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by a mutation in the WAS gene. The defective WAS protein leads to impaired function and survival of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, and platelets. The immunodeficiency results in susceptibility to recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. The thrombocytopenia is characterized by the presence of abnormally small platelets (micro thrombocytopenia) and leads to an increased risk of bleeding, which can manifest as petechiae, purpura, or severe hemorrhage. The eczematous rash is often severe and difficult to control. This unique combination of eczema, immunodeficiency, and micro thrombocytopenia is pathognomonic for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

q: What does the capnograph image below depict?
o: Spontaneous respiration during controlled mechanical ventillation
ex: Spontaneous respiration during controlled mechanical ventillation The capnogram shows a normal waveform for expiration followed by a small, notched cleft in the descending part of the alveolar plateau, just before the start of the next inspiration. This specific notch is known as a curare cleft. It is seen in patients who are receiving mechanical ventilation and are paralyzed with neuromuscular blocking agents. The cleft represents the patient's first, small, diaphragmatic effort to take a spontaneous breath against the ventilator as the effects of the muscle relaxant begin to wear off. It indicates that the patient's neuromuscular blockade is no longer complete and they are beginning to breathe on their own. Therefore, this capnographic finding is a sign of returning spontaneous respiration and indicates that a further dose of muscle relaxant may be required. Cardiac oscillations are typically seen as smaller, regular ripples on the expiratory plateau.

q: Identify the item shown in the image.
ex: Female condom The image displays a female condom. It is a barrier method of contraception that is inserted into the vagina before intercourse. It is a soft, loose-fitting pouch made of polyurethane or nitrile. Unlike a male condom, it has two flexible rings. The inner, smaller ring is at the closed end of the pouch and is used for insertion and to hold the condom in place against the cervix. The outer, larger ring remains outside the vagina, covering the labia. The female condom works by lining the vagina and preventing sperm from entering the uterus. It also provides protection against sexually transmitted infections. It is an effective, female-controlled method of contraception. A male condom (B) is a sheath that is worn over the penis. Chaaya (C) is a non-hormonal oral contraceptive pill.

q: Which vaccine should be given after a disaster?
ex: Vaccination against tetanus In the aftermath of a natural disaster such as an earthquake or flood, there is a significantly increased risk of traumatic injuries, including cuts, lacerations, and crush injuries, from debris and unsafe conditions. These wounds are often contaminated with soil and dirt, which can contain spores of Clostridium tetani, the bacterium that causes tetanus. Therefore, one of the most important and recommended public health measures in a post-disaster setting is to ensure that injured individuals receive tetanus prophylaxis. This may involve administering a booster dose of the tetanus toxoid vaccine to those with an unclear or outdated vaccination history. Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) may also be given for heavily contaminated wounds. While there is a concern for water-borne diseases, mass vaccination campaigns against typhoid or cholera are generally not recommended as a first-line response; the priority is providing safe water and sanitation.

q: What is the MONICA project?
o: Multinational monitoring of trends and determinants in Cardiovascular Disease
Multinational monitoring of trends and determinants in Cerebrovascular Disease
Multinational monitoring of trends and determinants in Diabetes
Multinational monitoring of trends and determinants in Congenital Heart Disease
ex: Multinational monitoring of trends and determinants in Cardiovascular Disease The MONICA project was a major international collaborative study initiated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in the 1980s. The name MONICA is an acronym for MONItoring of trends and determinants in CArdiovascular disease. It was one of the largest epidemiological studies ever conducted, involving 38 centers in 21 countries over a 10-year period. The primary objectives of the project were to measure the trends in mortality and morbidity from cardiovascular diseases (specifically coronary heart disease and stroke) and to assess the extent to which these trends were related to changes in known risk factors (such as smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels) and changes in medical care (such as treatment of heart attacks and hypertension) within those diverse populations. It provided invaluable data on the global dynamics of the cardiovascular disease epidemic.

q: What is the period for which Extended Sickness Benefit (ESB) is provided for tuberculosis under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act?
ex: 2 years The Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act in India provides a range of social security benefits to insured workers. The Sickness Benefit provides cash payments to workers during periods of certified sickness for a maximum of 91 days. However, for certain long-term diseases that require prolonged treatment and absence from work, an Extended Sickness Benefit (ESB) is available after the initial 91 days are exhausted. Tuberculosis is one of the specified diseases eligible for ESB. An insured person suffering from tuberculosis is entitled to receive ESB for a period that may be extended up to two years. This extended benefit is provided to ensure financial support for the worker and their family during the long course of anti-tubercular treatment and recovery, encouraging treatment adherence.

q: A person presents 4 hours after sustaining a clean wound without laceration and has a history of receiving a tetanus vaccine 10 years ago. What should be the next step in management?
o: Full course Tetanus vaccine to be given
Full dose TT with TIG (Tetanus Immune Globulin)
ex: Single-dose TT The management of a wound for tetanus prophylaxis depends on both the nature of the wound and the patient's vaccination history. In this case, the patient has a clean, minor wound. His last dose of the tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccine was 10 years ago. According to standard immunization guidelines, immunity from the tetanus vaccine wanes over time, and a booster dose is recommended every 10 years. For a patient with a clean, minor wound whose last dose was 10 or more years ago, or if their vaccination history is unknown, the correct management is to administer a single booster dose of the TT vaccine. This will be sufficient to boost their antibody levels and provide adequate protection. Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) is not necessary for clean, minor wounds. A full primary course of the vaccine is only required for individuals who have not been adequately immunized in the past.

q: Which influenza virus strain was responsible for the most recent influenza pandemic?
ex: H1N1 The most recent influenza pandemic occurred in 2009. This global outbreak was caused by a novel strain of the influenza A virus. This new virus was a reassortant virus, containing a unique combination of genetic material from human, avian, and swine influenza viruses. It was officially designated as the Influenza A (H1N1)pdm09 virus. Because the population had little to no pre-existing immunity to this novel strain, it spread rapidly across the globe, leading the World Health Organization to declare a pandemic in June 2009. This virus, often referred to colloquially as swine flu, has since continued to circulate as a seasonal influenza strain. The H5N1 and H7N7 strains are avian influenza viruses that have caused sporadic human infections but have not led to a pandemic.

q: Mission Indradhanush primarily targets improvement in which of the following areas?
ex: Universal immunization Mission Indradhanush is a flagship public health initiative launched by the Government of India in December 2014. Its primary and singular focus is on strengthening and re-energizing the routine immunization program to achieve full immunization coverage for all children under the age of two and all pregnant women. The mission is aimed at addressing the issue of vaccination gaps, targeting populations that are unvaccinated or only partially vaccinated. The name Indradhanush, meaning rainbow, was initially chosen to represent the seven vaccine-preventable diseases it targeted : diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, measles, and hepatitis B. The program has since expanded to include additional vaccines as per the National Immunization Schedule. Subsequent phases, known as Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI), have been launched to accelerate progress in specific high-priority districts and urban areas, with the ultimate goal of achieving universal immunization and reducing child mortality from preventable diseases.

q: Which of the following techniques or methods is based on behavioral sciences?
ex: Management by objectives Management by Objectives (MBO) is a management model that is heavily based on principles from the behavioral sciences, particularly motivation theory. MBO aims to improve the performance of an organization by clearly defining objectives that are agreed upon by both management and employees. The core idea is that involving employees in goal setting and action planning will increase their commitment, motivation, and alignment with organizational goals. This participatory approach draws directly from behavioral science concepts like Douglas McGregor's Theory Y, which assumes that employees are internally motivated and enjoy their work. In contrast, network analysis (like PERT and CPM) and systems analysis are quantitative management techniques derived from operations research and systems theory, focusing on processes and structures rather than human behavior. Decision making is a general process, not a specific technique based on behavioral sciences.

q: According to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), what is the target maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in terms of maternal deaths?
ex: < 70 per 1 lakh live births The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 global goals established by the United Nations in 2015. SDG 3 is focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all at all ages. Target 3.1 of this goal specifically addresses maternal mortality. The target states : By 2030, reduce the global maternal mortality ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births. This global target is a key benchmark for improving maternal healthcare, including access to skilled birth attendants, emergency obstetric care, and family planning services worldwide. The goal aims to ensure that no country has an MMR more than twice the global average. Options C and D express the rate per 1,000 live births, which is an incorrect denominator for the standard reporting of MMR, and the values are also incorrect.

q: Which parameter is most suitable for routine monitoring of air pollution?
o: Sulphur dioxide, smoke, and particulate matter
Sulphur dioxide, hydrogen sulphide, carbon monoxide
Sulphur dioxide, lead, and particulate matter NODIA 464=== (D) Between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
ex: Between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus The barium swallow image shows a Zenker's diverticulum, which is a pharyngoesophageal diverticulum. This is a false diverticulum (a pulsion diverticulum) where the mucosa and submucosa herniate through a weak spot in the posterior pharyngeal wall. This specific area of weakness is known as Killian's triangle. Killian's triangle is an anatomical weak point located in the posterior wall of the hypopharynx, situated between the two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle : the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle superiorly and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle inferiorly. Dysfunctional relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle during swallowing leads to increased intraluminal pressure in the hypopharynx, which forces the mucosa to herniate through this weak point, forming the diverticulum. Therefore, the most common site of origin is this specific area between the two components of the inferior constrictor muscle.

q: The bluish-purple discoloration observed behind the mastoid region, as shown in the image, is referred to as what clinical sign?
ex: Battle sign The image displays ecchymosis, or bruising, located in the postauricular region, over the mastoid process. This specific clinical finding is known as Battle's sign. The presence of Battle's sign is highly suggestive of a basilar skull fracture, specifically a fracture involving the middle cranial fossa and the petrous portion of the temporal bone. The fracture tears small blood vessels, and the blood then tracks along the path of the posterior auricular artery to pool in the subcutaneous tissue behind the ear, creating the visible bruise. It is a delayed sign, typically appearing 24 to 48 hours after the head injury. Its presence, often along with raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), is a strong indicator of a serious skull base fracture and warrants urgent neurosurgical evaluation and imaging. A Bezold abscess (B) is a deep neck abscess that is a complication of mastoiditis.

q: A patient presents with fever and difficulty in swallowing, and the image shows medial displacement of the tonsil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Peritonsillar abscess The clinical triad of fever, severe sore throat/dysphagia, and trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), along with the physical finding of a unilateral peritonsillar swelling that displaces the tonsil medially and pushes the uvula to the contralateral side, is classic for a peritonsillar abscess, also known as quinsy. This is a collection of pus that forms in the potential space between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, usually as a complication of acute tonsillitis. The image shows this characteristic pushing tonsil, where the affected tonsil and the overlying swollen soft palate are being pushed towards the midline by the underlying abscess. This is a common deep neck space infection that requires prompt drainage (either by needle aspiration or incision and drainage) and antibiotic therapy to prevent airway compromise or spread to deeper neck spaces.

q: A patient presents with a one-week history of toothache, and the clinical appearance is shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Ludwig's angina The image shows a patient with significant swelling and erythema in the submental and submandibular regions, giving a bull neck appearance. This, combined with the history of a recent toothache, is the classic presentation of Ludwig's angina. Ludwig's angina is a severe, rapidly progressive, and potentially life-threatening cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. The infection is typically odontogenic, most commonly arising from an infected lower molar tooth (especially the second or third molars). The infection spreads bilaterally into the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. This leads to a firm, woody induration of the floor of the mouth, elevation of the tongue, and massive swelling of the neck. The most significant danger is posterior displacement of the tongue, leading to acute airway obstruction. It is a surgical emergency that requires immediate airway management and aggressive antibiotic therapy.

q: What is the term used for widening of the cartilaginous portion of the external auditory canal?
ex: Meatoplasty A meatoplasty is a surgical procedure specifically designed to widen the meatus, or opening, of the external auditory canal. It is often performed in conjunction with mastoidectomy or other middle ear surgeries to improve aeration and drainage, allow for easier post-operative cleaning and inspection of the mastoid cavity, and prevent the accumulation of debris that can lead to recurrent infections. The procedure typically involves removing a portion of the conchal cartilage and surrounding soft tissue to enlarge the entrance to the canal. Tympanoplasty (C) is a broader term for the surgical reconstruction of the eardrum and/or the ossicular chain. Myringoplasty (B) specifically refers to the repair of a perforated eardrum. Otoplasty (A) is a cosmetic procedure to alter the shape or position of the external ear (pinna).

q: Which of the following features is not typical of tuberculous otitis media?
ex: Painful otorrhea Tuberculous otitis media is a rare form of chronic suppurative otitis media caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It has several classic clinical features that distinguish it from the more common pyogenic forms. One of its most defining characteristics is a painless, profuse, and persistent otorrhea (ear discharge). The lack of pain, despite significant tissue destruction, is a major clinical clue. Other classic findings include the presence of multiple perforations of the tympanic membrane which may later coalesce, pale and sluggish granulations in the middle ear cleft, and severe destruction of the ossicular chain, leading to a significant conductive hearing loss. Facial nerve palsy is also more common than in typical otitis media. Therefore, painful otorrhea is the feature that is not characteristic; the discharge is classically described as painless.

q: Partial or complete closure of the nasal cavity is performed as a treatment for which condition?
ex: Atrophic rhinitis Atrophic rhinitis (ozena) is a chronic nasal condition characterized by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa and turbinate bones, leading to a paradoxically wide nasal cavity filled with foul-smelling crusts. The goal of surgical treatment is to narrow the abnormally wide nasal cavity to reduce crust formation and improve mucosal function. Young's operation is a surgical procedure that involves creating mucocutaneous flaps to achieve a complete closure of the nostril. The nostril is kept closed for several months to a year, allowing the nasal mucosa to rest, regenerate, and reverse some of the atrophic changes. A modified version of the procedure involves only a partial closure. These surgical narrowing procedures are specific to the management of severe, recalcitrant atrophic rhinitis and are not used for other forms of rhinitis like allergic or vasomotor rhinitis.

q: What is the name given to the occipitofrontal view on an X-ray of the paranasal sinuses (PNS)?
ex: Caldwell view Plain X-rays for evaluating the paranasal sinuses involve specific projections to visualize the different sinuses without overlap. The occipitofrontal view, more commonly known as the Caldwell view, is a standard projection used for this purpose. It is taken with the patient's nose and forehead pressed against the film cassette and the X-ray beam angled at approximately 15 degrees caudally. This specific angulation projects the dense petrous ridges below the floor of the maxillary sinuses, providing an excellent, unobstructed view of the frontal sinuses and the ethmoid sinuses. In contrast, the Water's view (occipitomental view) is designed to provide the best visualization of the maxillary sinuses.
