q: What is the recommended treatment for intractable Sydenham chorea?
ex: Valproate Sydenham's chorea is a major neurological manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, resulting from an autoimmune reaction involving the basal ganglia. It presents with choreiform (rapid, involuntary, purposeless) movements, emotional lability, and hypotonia. While many cases are self-limiting, severe or intractable chorea requires pharmacological treatment. The current first-line treatment and drug of choice for Sydenham's chorea is sodium valproate. It has been shown to be effective in controlling the abnormal movements and has a more favorable safety profile compared to older agents. Haloperidol, a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist, is also effective but is now considered a second-line option due to the higher risk of acute extrapyramidal side effects and the potential for long-term tardive dyskinesia. Risperidone, an atypical antipsychotic, may also be used. Warfarin is an anticoagulant and is not used to treat the chorea itself.

q: Which of the following is not a diagnostic criterion for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)?
ex: Acoustic neuromas Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), also known as von Recklinghausen's disease, is diagnosed based on a set of specific clinical criteria established by the National Institutes of Health. A diagnosis requires two or more of the following : Six or more café-au-lait macules of a specific size. Two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma. Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions (Crowe's sign). An optic pathway glioma (a type of brain tumor). Two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas). A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or pseudoarthrosis of a long bone. A first-degree relative with NF1. Bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) are the hallmark and a diagnostic criterion for Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), not NF1. Therefore, acoustic neuromas are not a criterion for diagnosing NF1.

q: Which site is most commonly affected by chronic gastric ulcers?
ex: Lower part of lesser curvature Chronic peptic ulcers can occur in the stomach (gastric ulcers) or the duodenum. Within the stomach, gastric ulcers have a strong predilection for a specific location. The vast majority of benign gastric ulcers occur along the lesser curvature of the stomach. The most common site is at the junction of the acid-secreting body and the gastrin-producing antrum, known as the incisura angularis, which is on the lower part of the lesser curvature. The reasons for this localization are thought to be related to the Magenstrasse or gastric canal, a channel along the lesser curvature where gastric contents flow, leading to prolonged mucosal exposure to acid and pepsin. Ulcers on the greater curvature are much less common and have a higher likelihood of being malignant. The pyloric antrum is also a common site, but the incisura on the lesser curve is the most classic location.

q: What is the most appropriate diagnostic method for the clinical sign shown in the image?
ex: Serum ceruloplasmin The image displays a Kayser-Fleischer ring, a pathognomonic sign of Wilson's disease, an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. The diagnosis of Wilson's disease is based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory tests. One of the most important initial diagnostic tests is the measurement of serum ceruloplasmin. Ceruloplasmin is the main copper-carrying protein in the blood, synthesized in the liver. In about 90-95% of patients with Wilson's disease, the level of serum ceruloplasmin is markedly decreased. This is because the underlying genetic defect (in the ATP7B gene) impairs the incorporation of copper into apoceruloplasmin to form the final protein, leading to its rapid degradation. The combination of a low serum ceruloplasmin level with an increased 24-hour urinary copper excretion is highly suggestive of the diagnosis. Total serum copper can be misleadingly low because most copper is bound to ceruloplasmin. Karyotyping and PCR are genetic tests not used for initial biochemical diagnosis.

q: What is the approximate time interval between initial HIV infection and the development of AIDS?
ex: 10 years The natural history of an untreated HIV infection follows a predictable course. After the initial primary infection, there is a long period of clinical latency. During this phase, the virus continues to replicate, and there is a progressive decline in the number of CD4+ T-lymphocytes. Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is the final stage of HIV infection, defined by the development of certain opportunistic infections, specific cancers, or a severe drop in the CD4 count to below 200 cells/mm³. In the absence of antiretroviral therapy (ART), the median time from initial HIV infection to the development of clinical AIDS is approximately 8 to 10 years. This time interval can vary significantly among individuals based on factors like the viral load, host genetics, and co-infections. With the widespread availability and use of effective ART, the progression to AIDS can be prevented, and individuals with HIV can have a near-normal life expectancy.

q: Heller's myotomy is done for which condition?
ex: Achalasia cardia Achalasia cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by two key features : impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) upon swallowing and the absence of normal peristalsis in the body of the esophagus. This leads to a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction, causing symptoms like dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), regurgitation, and chest pain. The Heller myotomy is the standard surgical treatment for achalasia. The procedure involves making a longitudinal incision through the muscle layers (myotomy) of the distal esophagus and the proximal stomach, specifically cutting through the hypertonic lower esophageal sphincter muscle. This relieves the obstruction and allows food to pass more easily into the stomach. The procedure is usually performed laparoscopically and is often combined with an anti-reflux procedure (fundoplication) to prevent postoperative gastroesophageal reflux. Zenker's diverticulum is treated with a diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeal myotomy.

q: A 35-year-old woman shows myocardial stunning on imaging, yet her ECG does not display typical ischemic patterns. What is the most probable diagnosis?
ex: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as stress cardiomyopathy or broken heart syndrome, is an acute and transient form of cardiac dysfunction that typically affects postmenopausal women and is often precipitated by intense emotional or physical stress. It clinically mimics an acute myocardial infarction, with patients presenting with chest pain and shortness of breath. However, coronary angiography reveals no significant coronary artery disease. The hallmark of the condition is a characteristic pattern of regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography or ventriculography, showing apical ballooning of the left ventricle with basal hyperkinesis. This appearance resembles a takotsubo, a Japanese octopus trapping pot. The ECG changes can be variable and often do not conform to a specific coronary territory, and cardiac enzyme elevation is typically modest. The myocardial stunning and atypical ECG changes in a patient without coronary artery disease are classic for this diagnosis.

q: Which drug can be used as an alternative during cardiac arrest if epinephrine is unavailable?
ex: High-dose Vasopressin In the Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) algorithms for cardiac arrest, epinephrine is the primary vasopressor used to increase coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during CPR. However, for a period, the guidelines included vasopressin as an alternative or in combination with epinephrine. Vasopressin is a potent non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor that acts on V1 receptors. A single dose of 40 units of vasopressin could be used to replace either the first or second dose of epinephrine in the treatment of pulseless electrical activity (PEA), asystole, or ventricular fibrillation. While more recent guideline updates have removed vasopressin from the main algorithm due to studies showing no superior benefit over epinephrine, it was historically recognized as a valid alternative vasopressor in cardiac arrest. Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic. Atropine is used for bradycardia. Adenosine is for supraventricular tachycardia.

q: A patient has cutaneous vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, and peripheral neuropathy. Which investigation should be done next to aid in diagnosing the condition?
ex: ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies) The clinical triad of cutaneous vasculitis (e.g., palpable purpura), glomerulonephritis (causing hematuria and proteinuria), and peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) is highly suggestive of a systemic small-vessel vasculitis. The most important initial investigation to differentiate between the types of small-vessel vasculitis is testing for Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (ANCA). ANCA-associated vasculitides include Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA), and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss). A positive c-ANCA (anti-PR3) is highly specific for GPA, while a positive p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is typically seen in MPA. The results of the ANCA test are crucial for establishing a diagnosis and guiding treatment with immunosuppressive therapy. While HBsAg can be associated with polyarteritis nodosa (a medium-vessel vasculitis), the presentation is more classic for an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis.

q: Which organism is the most common cause of acute bacterial prostatitis?
ex: E.coli Acute bacterial prostatitis is an infection of the prostate gland characterized by fever, chills, pelvic pain, and urinary symptoms. The causative pathogens are typically the same bacteria that cause urinary tract infections (UTIs). By far, the most common organism responsible for acute bacterial prostatitis is Escherichia coli (E. coli), accounting for approximately 80% of all cases. Other less common Gram-negative bacteria from the Enterobacteriaceae family, such as Klebsiella and Proteus, can also be involved. Gram-positive bacteria, such as Enterococcus, are a much less frequent cause. The infection usually occurs via an ascending route from the urethra or by reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts. The predominance of E. coli reflects its status as the most common uropathogen. Streptococcus viridans is part of the oral flora, and Peptostreptococcus is an anaerobe, both of which are rare causes of this condition.

q: Which of the following organisms produces histamine responsible for causing scombroid fish poisoning?
ex: Morganella morganii Scombroid fish poisoning is a type of foodborne illness that occurs after consumption of improperly stored fish, particularly dark-meat fish such as tuna, mackerel, or bonito. When these fish are not adequately refrigerated, certain bacteria proliferate and convert histidine naturally present in fish muscle into histamine through the enzyme histidine decarboxylase. Morganella morganii is one of the most important histamine-producing bacteria implicated in this process. Ingestion of histamine-rich fish leads to symptoms resembling an allergic reaction, including flushing, headache, palpitations, sweating, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes bronchospasm. Symptoms typically begin within minutes to a few hours after consumption and are usually self-limited. Proper refrigeration of fish prevents bacterial growth and histamine formation. Other listed organisms are not classically associated with scombroid poisoning.

q: Who is recognized as the Father of Microbiology?
ex: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek Antonie van Leeuwenhoek is widely regarded as the Father of Microbiology because he was the first person to observe and accurately describe microorganisms using handcrafted microscopes of exceptional quality. In the late 17th century, he examined samples of pond water, dental plaque, blood, and other materials, discovering bacteria, protozoa, sperm cells, and red blood cells—organisms he called “animalcules.” His meticulous observations opened an entirely new world of life invisible to the naked eye and laid the foundation for microbiology as a scientific discipline. Although scientists like Louis Pasteur and Robert Brown made major later contributions—such as germ theory and cell studies—Leeuwenhoek’s pioneering microscopic discoveries came first. Therefore, he is most appropriately honored as the Father of Microbiology.

q: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by which organism?
ex: Ancylostoma braziliense Cutaneous larva migrans, also known as creeping eruption, is a parasitic skin infection characterized by an intensely pruritic, erythematous, and serpiginous (snake-like) track that moves over time. The condition is caused by the accidental penetration of human skin by the filariform larvae of animal hookworms. The most common causative agent is Ancylostoma braziliense, the hookworm of dogs and cats. Humans become infected when they walk barefoot or lie on soil or sand contaminated with the feces of infected animals. The larvae penetrate the skin but are unable to complete their life cycle in humans because they lack the necessary collagenase enzymes to break through the basement membrane of the dermis. They are therefore trapped in the epidermis and wander, creating the characteristic migratory tracks. Necator americanus is a human hookworm that can penetrate the skin but then migrates to the lungs and intestines. Toxocara canis causes visceral or ocular larva migrans. Strongyloides can cause a different condition called larva currens.

q: What action does the muscle shown in the picture produce at the MCP joint?
ex: Flexion The muscle shown in the image represents the interossei muscles of the hand. These muscles lie between the metacarpal bones and insert into the base of the proximal phalanges as well as the extensor expansion. Although the interossei are commonly remembered for their role in adduction and abduction of the fingers (PAD – Palmar interossei Adduct, DAB – Dorsal interossei Abduct), their important action at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint is flexion. At the MCP joint, both dorsal and palmar interossei flex the proximal phalanges. At the same time, through their attachment to the extensor expansion, they assist in extension of the interphalangeal (IP) joints. Since the question specifically asks for the action at the MCP joint, the correct response is flexion, not adduction. Adduction refers to movement of the fingers toward the midline of the hand, but that is not the primary movement being tested here. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) Flexion.

q: Which organism is most likely to cause infection following a kidney transplant?
ex: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Patients who undergo solid organ transplantation, such as a kidney transplant, require long-term immunosuppressive therapy to prevent graft rejection. This chronic state of immunosuppression makes them highly susceptible to a wide range of opportunistic infections. Among viral pathogens, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most significant and common causes of morbidity and mortality in these patients. Infection can occur as a primary infection (if a CMV-negative recipient receives an organ from a CMV-positive donor), a reactivation of the recipient's latent CMV, or a superinfection with a new strain. CMV disease can manifest as a systemic febrile illness, or it can directly affect the transplanted organ (CMV nephritis) or other organ systems, causing pneumonitis, colitis, or retinitis. Because it is so common and can have severe consequences, routine monitoring for CMV viremia and prophylactic or pre-emptive antiviral therapy (e.g., with valganciclovir) is a standard part of post-transplant care. While bacterial infections also occur, CMV is the most characteristic viral pathogen in this setting.

q: In a child with sickle cell anemia who develops multiple nonsuppurative osteomyelitis, which organism is the most likely cause?
ex: Salmonella Osteomyelitis is a well-recognized complication of sickle cell disease due to repeated vaso-occlusion, bone infarction, and impaired immune function. Infarcted bone becomes highly susceptible to infection, particularly by enteric organisms. Among these, Salmonella species are classically associated with osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia, making this a high-yield clinical association. The bacteria likely reach bone via the bloodstream following translocation from the gastrointestinal tract. In contrast, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in the general population but is less characteristic in sickle cell disease. Patients typically present with fever, localized bone pain, swelling, and reduced limb movement. Early diagnosis and prompt antibiotic therapy are essential to prevent complications such as chronic osteomyelitis, bone destruction, and growth disturbances. Thus, Salmonella is the most likely causative organism in this scenario.

q: Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with infection by Parvovirus B19?
o: Aplastic anemia in sickle cell disease
ex: Roseola infantum Parvovirus B19 is a DNA virus that primarily infects erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow, leading to several characteristic clinical conditions. It is the causative agent of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), a common childhood illness marked by a “slapped-cheek” facial rash and mild fever. In individuals with underlying hemolytic disorders such as sickle cell disease, Parvovirus B19 can cause transient aplastic crisis due to suppression of red blood cell production, resulting in severe anemia. Infection during pregnancy may lead to fetal hydrops because of profound fetal anemia and heart failure. In contrast, roseola infantum (exanthem subitum) is caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), and less commonly HHV-7, not Parvovirus B19. Roseola typically presents with high fever followed by a sudden maculopapular rash as the fever subsides. Therefore, roseola infantum is not caused by Parvovirus B19.

q: In Bartter syndrome, which segment of the nephron is affected?
o: Defect in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
ex: Defect in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle Bartter syndrome is a group of rare, inherited salt-wasting tubulopathies characterized by hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria, and normal to low blood pressure, despite high levels of renin and aldosterone. The underlying genetic defect in classic Bartter syndrome involves one of several ion transporters located in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle. The most common form (Type I) is due to a mutation in the gene for the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2). Other forms involve mutations in the ROMK potassium channel or the basolateral chloride channel (CLC-Kb). The dysfunction of these transporters impairs the reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride in the TAL. This leads to a loss of these salts in the urine, volume depletion, and secondary hyperaldosteronism, which drives the potassium and hydrogen ion loss. The effect is similar to taking a loop diuretic like furosemide, which also targets the NKCC2 transporter.

q: Pseudo P-pulmonale is due to?
ex: Hypokalemia P-pulmonale is an ECG finding characterized by tall, peaked P waves (amplitude > 2.5 mm) in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). It is classically a sign of right atrial enlargement (right atriopathy), often seen in patients with chronic pulmonary diseases like COPD. However, a similar ECG pattern, termed pseudo P-pulmonale, can be observed in the absence of true right atrial enlargement. This pattern can be caused by several factors, most notably electrolyte disturbances. Severe hypokalemia (low serum potassium) is a well-known cause of pseudo P-pulmonale. The low potassium levels can alter the cardiac action potentials and repolarization patterns. Other ECG changes in hypokalemia include flattened T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression, and prolongation of the QT interval. The P wave changes in this context are a reflection of the electrolyte imbalance rather than structural heart disease. q: Mycoplasma is resistant to:
ex: Ceftriaxone Mycoplasma species are a unique type of bacteria that are intrinsically resistant to a major class of antibiotics. The defining characteristic of Mycoplasma is that they completely lack a cell wall. Antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis for their mechanism of action are therefore completely ineffective against them. This includes all beta-lactam antibiotics, such as penicillins and cephalosporins. Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin and acts by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. Since Mycoplasma has no cell wall to target, it is naturally resistant to ceftriaxone. In contrast, Mycoplasma infections are treated with antibiotics that target other bacterial processes. These include tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) and macrolides (e.g., azithromycin), which inhibit protein synthesis by acting on the ribosome, and fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin), which inhibit DNA synthesis. Aminoglycosides also inhibit protein synthesis.

q: Which medication reduces bone breakdown in osteoporosis?
ex: Risedronate Risedronate reduces bone breakdown in osteoporosis by inhibiting osteoclast activity. Osteoporosis is characterized by an imbalance between bone resorption (breakdown) and bone formation, leading to fragile bones and increased fracture risk. Osteoclasts are the cells responsible for bone resorption. Risedronate belongs to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates, which bind strongly to bone mineral and suppress osteoclast-mediated bone destruction. As a result, bone density increases and fracture risk decreases. Teriparatide (A) works differently; it is a recombinant form of parathyroid hormone that stimulates new bone formation by activating osteoblasts, so it promotes bone building rather than reducing breakdown. Cortisone (C) actually worsens osteoporosis because long-term corticosteroid use accelerates bone loss and decreases calcium absorption. Cimetidine (D) is an H₂-receptor antagonist used for peptic ulcer disease and has no significant role in bone metabolism. Therefore, among the given options, risedronate is the medication specifically designed to reduce bone resorption and slow the progression of osteoporosis.

q: Allopurinol lowers uric acid by which mechanism?
o: Promotion of uric acid excretion via renal tubules
Inhibition of the enzyme xanthine oxidase
ex: Inhibition of the enzyme xanthine oxidase Allopurinol lowers uric acid levels by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase, which plays a key role in purine metabolism. Normally, purines from dietary sources and cell turnover are broken down into hypoxanthine and xanthine, which are then converted into uric acid by xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol is a structural analog of hypoxanthine and acts as a competitive inhibitor of this enzyme. By blocking xanthine oxidase, it prevents the formation of uric acid, leading to reduced serum urate levels. Instead, hypoxanthine and xanthine—more water-soluble compounds—accumulate and are excreted more easily by the kidneys. This mechanism makes allopurinol especially useful in the long-term management of gout and in conditions associated with excessive uric acid production, such as tumor lysis syndrome. Option (A) describes uricosuric drugs (e.g., probenecid), (C) relates to NSAIDs, and (D) refers to urine alkalinizing agents. Only option (B) correctly explains allopurinol’s action.

q: Besides epinephrine, which medication is recommended for ventricular fibrillation during cardiac arrest?
ex: Amiodarone Amiodarone is recommended, in addition to epinephrine, for the treatment of ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia during cardiac arrest that is unresponsive to defibrillation. VF is a life-threatening arrhythmia characterized by chaotic electrical activity in the ventricles, resulting in no effective cardiac output. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug that prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractory period, helping to stabilize the cardiac membrane and restore a normal rhythm. Dopamine (B) is mainly used for hemodynamic support in shock and severe hypotension, not for VF during arrest. Adenosine (C) is used to treat certain supraventricular tachycardias, not ventricular fibrillation. Atropine (D) is used for symptomatic bradycardia and is no longer recommended for asystole or pulseless electrical activity in cardiac arrest protocols. Therefore, amiodarone is the preferred antiarrhythmic medication for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation during cardiac arrest.

q: Which statement regarding vitamin K is correct?
o: Prolonged use of antimicrobials leads to deficiency
ex: Prolonged use of antimicrobials leads to deficiency Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver, as well as proteins C and S. It plays a crucial role in blood coagulation, promoting clot formation rather than preventing it. Therefore, option (A) is incorrect because vitamin K is not an anticoagulant; instead, it has a procoagulant effect. A significant portion of vitamin K (especially vitamin K₂) is produced by normal intestinal bacteria. Prolonged use of broad-spectrum antimicrobials can disrupt gut flora, reducing endogenous vitamin K production and potentially leading to deficiency. This deficiency may result in bleeding tendencies due to impaired clotting factor synthesis, making option (B) correct. Option (C) is incorrect because the daily dietary requirement of vitamin K is in micrograms (about 55–120 µg/day for adults), not milligrams. Since statements (A) and (C) are false, option (D) cannot be correct. Thus, prolonged antimicrobial therapy is a recognized cause of vitamin K deficiency.

q: Use of which drug necessitates regular monitoring of prothrombin time (PT/INR)?
ex: Coumadin Coumadin is the brand name of Warfarin, an oral anticoagulant that requires regular monitoring of prothrombin time (PT), expressed as the international normalized ratio (INR). Warfarin works by inhibiting vitamin K–dependent synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver. Because its anticoagulant effect can vary widely due to diet, drug interactions, liver function, and genetics, careful monitoring is essential to maintain therapeutic efficacy while preventing bleeding complications. If the INR is too low, there is a risk of thrombosis; if too high, there is a risk of serious bleeding. Therefore, periodic PT/INR testing guides dose adjustments. Aspirin (A) affects platelet function and does not require PT/INR monitoring. Lepirudin (B), a direct thrombin inhibitor, is monitored using activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), not PT/INR. Digoxin (C) is a cardiac glycoside used in heart failure and arrhythmias and requires serum drug level monitoring, not coagulation tests. Thus, Coumadin (warfarin) is the drug that necessitates regular PT/INR monitoring.

q: Trichloroethylene (Trilene) undergoes breakdown primarily through which process?
ex: Enzymatic degradation Trichloroethylene (TCE), also known as Trilene, is primarily broken down in the body through enzymatic metabolism in the liver. The main pathway involves hepatic microsomal enzymes, especially cytochrome P450 oxidases. These enzymes convert trichloroethylene into several metabolites, including chloral hydrate, trichloroethanol, and trichloroacetic acid, which are then excreted in urine. This process represents enzymatic degradation because it depends on specific biological enzymes rather than simple chemical reactions. Environmental hydrolysis (B) is not a major pathway for TCE breakdown in the body. Chemical oxidation (C) can occur in industrial or environmental settings but is not the primary mechanism in human metabolism. Option (D) is incorrect because trichloroethylene is indeed metabolized and eliminated from the body rather than remaining unchanged. Therefore, the principal route of trichloroethylene breakdown in humans is enzyme-mediated metabolism in the liver, making enzymatic degradation the correct answer.

q: A posthumous child is:
o: Child delivered after death of biological mother
Child delivered after death of biological father
ex: Child delivered after death of biological father The term posthumous is derived from the Latin postumus, meaning last, and in this context, it refers to something that occurs or is published after someone's death. In legal and common language, a posthumous child is specifically defined as a child who is born after the death of their biological father. This situation has significant legal implications, particularly concerning matters of inheritance, succession, and legitimacy. Most legal systems have provisions to ensure that a posthumous child is granted the same rights as a child born during the father's lifetime. For example, the child is generally considered an heir to the deceased father's estate. The term does not apply to a child delivered after the mother's death (which would typically involve a postmortem cesarean section) or after both parents' deaths, although the word could be used more broadly in a non-legal sense. Abandonment by parents is a separate social and legal issue.

q: Under which section of the Indian Penal Code is the M'Naghten Rule—used to establish the legal defense of insanity—codified?
ex: Convergent Muscle architecture is classified based on the arrangement of its fascicles. The image shows the pectoralis major muscle, which is a classic example of a convergent muscle. In a convergent muscle, the fascicles originate from a broad, fan-shaped area and then converge or narrow down to insert onto a single, small tendon. This arrangement allows for versatility in the direction of pull and generates a large amount of force, although it compromises on the range of motion compared to parallel muscles. The pectoralis major's broad origin on the clavicle and sternum and its narrow insertion on the humerus perfectly illustrate this convergent or triangular pattern. A parallel muscle has fascicles that run parallel to the long axis (e.g., sartorius). A pennate muscle has short fascicles that attach obliquely to a central tendon (unipennate, bipennate, or multipennate like the deltoid).

q: Which of the following conditions lead to hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis accompanied by hypertension?
ex: Liddle syndrome The combination of hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (low potassium, high bicarbonate) and hypertension is a key finding that points towards a state of mineralocorticoid excess or apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Liddle syndrome is a rare, autosomal dominant genetic disorder that perfectly fits this profile. It is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the genes for the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting ducts of the kidney. This mutation leads to constitutive, unregulated reabsorption of sodium, independent of aldosterone. The excessive sodium reabsorption causes volume expansion and severe hypertension. It also creates a negative electrical potential in the tubular lumen, which drives the secretion and subsequent loss of potassium and hydrogen ions, resulting in hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. A key feature is that renin and aldosterone levels are suppressed. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes cause hypokalemic alkalosis but with normal or low blood pressure.

q: Which condition may not benefit from oxygen therapy?
ex: Subglottic stenosis Oxygen therapy is beneficial in conditions where hypoxemia results from impaired gas exchange at the alveolar level. In asthma, oxygen helps correct hypoxia caused by bronchospasm and ventilation–perfusion mismatch. In pneumonia, alveoli are filled with inflammatory exudate, impairing oxygen diffusion, so supplemental oxygen improves arterial oxygenation. In pulmonary fibrosis, thickening of the alveolar membrane reduces diffusion capacity, and oxygen therapy increases the oxygen gradient, improving blood oxygen levels. However, subglottic stenosis is an upper airway obstruction located below the vocal cords. The primary issue is mechanical narrowing of the airway, not impaired oxygen diffusion. Simply giving oxygen does not relieve the obstruction. These patients require airway management such as nebulization, steroids, dilation, or possibly surgical intervention. While oxygen may be given temporarily, it does not correct the underlying problem. Therefore, the condition that may not significantly benefit from oxygen therapy is (C) Subglottic stenosis.

q: The following chemical structure represents which compound?
ex: 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) The chemical structure shown is that of serotonin. Serotonin is a monoamine neurotransmitter, and its chemical name is 5-hydroxytryptamine, commonly abbreviated as 5-HT. q: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block occurs in all of the following conditions, except which one?
ex: Respiratory failure Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block is characterized by intermittent non-conducted P waves without progressive PR interval prolongation. It usually indicates disease of the His–Purkinje system and is considered more serious than Mobitz type 1 because it may progress to complete heart block. Myocardial infarction, particularly anterior wall MI, can damage the conduction system and produce Mobitz type 2 block. Fibrosis of the conduction system, commonly seen in elderly patients (Lev’s or Lenègre’s disease), is a classic cause. Hyperkalemia can also impair conduction through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, leading to various degrees of heart block, including Mobitz type 2. However, respiratory failure primarily affects oxygenation and carbon dioxide levels. While severe hypoxia may cause arrhythmias, it is not a typical or direct cause of Mobitz type 2 AV block. Therefore, the correct answer is (D) Respiratory failure.

q: What is the recommended drug regimen for a pregnant woman diagnosed with HIV infection?

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) with either emtricitabine (FTC) or lamivudine (3TC) are commonly used and considered safe in pregnancy. q: What is the earliest clinical sign of third cranial nerve involvement in a patient with diabetes mellitus?
ex: Normal light and accommodation reflex In patients with diabetes mellitus, third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy is commonly caused by microvascular ischemia affecting the central core of the nerve. The oculomotor nerve contains motor fibers centrally and parasympathetic (pupillary) fibers peripherally. In diabetic third nerve palsy, the central motor fibers are affected first, leading to ptosis and limitation of eye movements (ophthalmoplegia). However, the peripheral parasympathetic fibers that control the pupil are usually spared because they receive a richer blood supply. As a result, the pupil remains normal, and both the light reflex and accommodation reflex are preserved in the early stages. This phenomenon is known as pupil-sparing third nerve palsy, which is characteristic of diabetic ischemic neuropathy. In contrast, compressive lesions (such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm) typically affect the peripheral parasympathetic fibers first, leading to an abnormal light reflex. Therefore, the earliest clinical finding is (C) Normal light and accommodation reflex.

q: What value of BMI should be considered "lethal" in men? NODIA 672===
ex: 12 Body Mass Index (BMI) is a simple measure used to assess body weight relative to height and is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m²). In adult men, a normal BMI ranges from 18.5 to 24.9. A BMI below 18.5 is considered underweight, and values below 16 indicate severe malnutrition. When BMI falls to extremely low levels such as 12, it is considered life-threatening or “lethal.” At a BMI of around 12, the body has critically low fat and muscle stores. This leads to severe protein–energy malnutrition, weakened immunity, electrolyte imbalance, cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension, hypothermia, and multi-organ dysfunction. The heart muscle becomes weak, increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. Such low BMI levels are commonly seen in advanced anorexia nervosa or prolonged starvation and are associated with very high mortality rates. In contrast, BMI values such as 13 or 14 are also extremely dangerous but may not always be immediately fatal with urgent medical intervention. Therefore, a BMI of 12 is considered the most lethal among the given options.

q: A disease has an incidence of 4 per 100 population and an average duration of 2 years. What is its prevalence?
ex: 8 per 1000 In stable epidemiological conditions (where incidence, duration, and population size are relatively constant), there is a well-established relationship between prevalence, incidence, and the duration of a disease. Prevalence refers to the total number of existing cases (new and old) in a population at a specific point in time, while incidence refers to the rate of new cases occurring over a period. The formula that connects these three variables is : Prevalence = Incidence × Average Duration of the Disease This formula is applicable for chronic diseases where the prevalence is low (typically less than 10%). Given the data in the question : Incidence = 4 cases per 1000 population per year. Average Duration = 2 years. Prevalence = (4 / 1000) × 2 = 8 / 1000. Therefore, the prevalence of the disease is estimated to be 8 per 1000 of the population. This means that at any given time, 8 out of every 1000 people in the population are expected to have the disease.

q: By which method are cytotoxic and expired drugs disposed of?
ex: Burning (Incineration) Cytotoxic drugs (antineoplastic or chemotherapy drugs) and expired pharmaceutical products are classified as hazardous biomedical waste. These substances are chemically reactive and potentially genotoxic, carcinogenic, or teratogenic, posing a significant risk to public health and the environment if not disposed of properly. The recommended and most effective method for the final disposal of this type of waste is high-temperature incineration. Incineration at temperatures typically above 850°C ensures the complete thermal destruction and decomposition of the active chemical compounds, rendering them inert and non-toxic. The resulting ash can then be safely disposed of in a secured landfill. Autoclaving is a sterilization method using steam, which is ineffective for chemical waste. Simply dumping or disposing in a standard landfill is prohibited as it would lead to the contamination of soil and groundwater. Therefore, secure incineration is the mandated method for destroying cytotoxic and expired drugs to prevent environmental contamination and public exposure.

q: What should the couple protection rate be for the Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) to equal 1?
ex: 60% The Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) is a demographic indicator that represents the average number of daughters that would be born to a woman (or a group of women) if she passed through her lifetime conforming to the age-specific fertility and mortality rates of a given year. An NRR of 1 signifies that each generation of mothers is producing exactly enough daughters to replace itself, leading to a stable population size over the long term (zero population growth). To achieve this replacement-level fertility, a certain proportion of couples in the reproductive age group must be using contraception. The Couple Protection Rate (CPR) is the percentage of eligible couples effectively protected against childbirth by one or another approved method of family planning. It has been estimated that a CPR of approximately 60% is required for a population to achieve an NRR of 1. This is a crucial target for national family planning programs aiming for population stabilization.

q: The CT scan of the thorax shown below is suggestive of which condition?
ex: Descending Aortic dissection The contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest provides a clear view of the aorta and is the gold standard for diagnosing aortic dissection. The image shows the descending thoracic aorta. The pathognomonic finding of an aortic dissection is visible : an intimal flap, which is a thin, linear structure representing the torn inner layer (intima) of the aorta. This flap separates the aortic lumen into two channels : the true lumen (where blood flows normally) and the false lumen (where blood has tracked into the aortic wall). This finding confirms the diagnosis of an aortic dissection. Since the dissection is seen in the descending aorta and the ascending aorta (which is located more anteriorly) appears normal, this represents a descending aortic dissection. According to the Stanford classification, this would be a Type B dissection. An ascending aortic dissection (Stanford Type A) would involve the aorta proximal to the left subclavian artery and is a surgical emergency.

q: What is the name of the new online RNTCP software used to monitor the TB control programme?
ex: NIKSHAY NIKSHAY (derived from Ni for end and Kshay for TB) is a web-based and mobile-based health information management system developed and implemented by the Government of India for the National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP), formerly known as RNTCP. It was launched in 2012 to comprehensively monitor and manage TB patients and control program activities across the country. NIKSHAY serves as a unified interface for all stakeholders, including public and private healthcare providers, laboratories, and program managers. It is used for the mandatory notification of all TB cases, tracking patients from diagnosis through treatment completion, managing drug supplies, and monitoring treatment adherence. The system also integrates features for direct benefit transfers (Nikshay Poshan Yojana) to support patients' nutritional needs. It is a critical digital tool in India's strategy to eliminate tuberculosis by 2025, enabling real-time surveillance and improving the quality of patient care and program management.

q: What is the study unit in an ecological study?
ex: Population In epidemiology, different study designs use different units of observation and analysis. In most study designs, such as case-control studies or cohort studies, the unit of analysis is the individual (e.g., a patient or a case). However, an ecological study (also known as a correlational study) is unique in that the unit of analysis is not the individual but an entire population or a group of people. These studies examine the relationship between an exposure and an outcome by using aggregate data for a population, rather than data on individual members. For example, an ecological study might correlate the average per capita cigarette sales in different countries with the age-adjusted mortality rates from lung cancer in those same countries. The key characteristic is that data is analyzed at the group level, making population the correct study unit. A major limitation of this design is the ecological fallacy—an association observed at the group level may not hold true for individuals.

q: In a diabetes mellitus (DM) screening program involving 1,000 individuals, 90 people tested positive on the screening test. However, a confirmatory gold-standard test showed that 100 individuals actually had the disease. What is the sensitivity of the screening test?
ex: 90/100 Sensitivity is a measure of a screening test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease. It is calculated as the proportion of true positives among all individuals who actually have the disease. The formula for sensitivity is : Sensitivity = (True Positives) / (True Positives + False Negatives) In this problem : The total number of people who truly have the disease (as determined by the gold standard test) is 100. This is the denominator (True Positives + False Negatives). The number of people who tested positive with the screening test is 90. This represents the True Positives. We can infer that 10 people who had the disease were missed by the screening test (100 total diseased - 90 who tested positive = 10 False Negatives). Therefore, the sensitivity of the screening test is calculated as : Sensitivity = 90 / (90 + 10) = 90 / 100. This means the test correctly identifies 90% of all people who actually have diabetes mellitus.

q: Which drug is used for mass chemoprophylaxis in meningococcal meningitis?
ex: Rifampicin Chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal meningitis is recommended for close contacts of a person with the disease to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis and prevent secondary cases. In situations of a large-scale outbreak, mass chemoprophylaxis may be considered. The drugs of choice for this purpose must be effective, easy to administer, and safe for large populations. Rifampicin has historically been a primary agent for mass chemoprophylaxis. It is highly effective at eradicating nasopharyngeal carriage and is given orally for two days. However, it has several contraindications (e.g., pregnancy, liver disease) and can lead to resistance. For this reason, other agents like ciprofloxacin (single oral dose) or ceftriaxone (single intramuscular injection) are now often preferred, especially for individual contacts. Nevertheless, rifampicin remains a recognized and effective option for mass prophylaxis. Penicillin is used for treatment, not prophylaxis, as it does not reliably eliminate the carrier state.

q: Which of the following represents the active form of chlorination?
ex: Hypochlorous acid Chlorination is the most common method of water disinfection. When chlorine is added to water, it reacts with the water to form two compounds : hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hydrochloric acid (HCl). The hypochlorous acid can then dissociate into a hypochlorite ion (OCl-) and a hydrogen ion (H+). The relative proportion of HOCl and OCl- depends on the pH of the water. Both hypochlorous acid and the hypochlorite ion have disinfecting properties, but hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is the much more potent and effective disinfecting agent. It is estimated to be about 80 to 100 times more effective at killing microorganisms than the hypochlorite ion. Therefore, water chlorination is most effective at a slightly acidic to neutral pH (below 7.5), which favors the formation of HOCl over OCl-. Chloride ion (Cl-) has no disinfectant properties. Hydrogen chloride (HCl) is a strong acid.

q: The ratio of risk in the exposed group to the risk in the unexposed group is referred to as what?
ex: Relative risk Relative Risk (RR), also known as the risk ratio, is a key measure of association used in epidemiological studies, particularly in cohort studies and randomized controlled trials. It quantifies the strength of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is calculated as the ratio of the incidence (or risk) of the outcome in the exposed group to the incidence of the outcome in the unexposed group. RR = [Incidence in the exposed] / [Incidence in the unexposed] An RR of 1 indicates no association. An RR greater than 1 indicates that the exposure increases the risk of the outcome (a risk factor). An RR less than 1 indicates that the exposure decreases the risk of the outcome (a protective factor). The odds ratio is a similar measure used in case-control studies. Attributable risk measures the excess risk due to the exposure.

q: What is the recommended interval between two live vaccines?
ex: 4 weeks The administration of live attenuated vaccines requires careful scheduling to ensure an optimal immune response. If two different live vaccines (e.g., MMR and Varicella) are not administered on the same day, a minimum interval must be maintained between them. The standard recommendation is that there should be a minimum gap of 4 weeks (or 28 days) between the administration of two different live parenteral (injected) or intranasal vaccines. The reason for this interval is to prevent immune interference. The immune response generated by the first live vaccine, particularly the production of interferons, can temporarily inhibit the replication of the second live virus vaccine if it is given too soon. This could lead to a suboptimal immune response and potential vaccine failure for the second vaccine. This rule does not apply to oral live vaccines like OPV or rotavirus vaccine, or to inactivated vaccines.

q: When a susceptible person develops a disease within the incubation period after exposure to the primary case, what is this called?
ex: Secondary attack rate The Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) is a measure of the infectivity or contagiousness of a disease and is used to evaluate control measures. It is defined as the number of new cases of a disease that occur among the susceptible contacts of a known primary case, within one incubation period of the disease. The formula is : SAR = (Number of new cases among contacts / Total number of susceptible contacts) × 100. This rate specifically measures the spread of a disease from the initial case (primary case) to those who were directly exposed to that case. It is a useful metric for investigating disease outbreaks in closed settings like households, schools, or barracks. The primary attack rate refers to the rate of disease among all those exposed during an outbreak. The case fatality rate is the proportion of cases that result in death.

q: Out of 100 women who were given oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for contraception, 10 became pregnant during a 24-month follow-up period. What is the Pearl Index?
ex: 5 The Pearl Index is a common statistical method used to measure the effectiveness of a birth control method. It calculates the number of accidental pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure. The formula for the Pearl Index is : Pearl Index = (Number of accidental pregnancies / Total months of exposure) × 1200 (The multiplication by 1200 converts the rate to pregnancies per 100 women observed for one year). In this problem : Number of women = 100 Number of accidental pregnancies = 10 Follow-up period = 24 months Total months of exposure = Number of women × Follow-up period = 100 × 24 = 2400 months. Pearl Index = (10 / 2400) × 1200 Pearl Index = 10 / 2 = 5. This means that if 100 women use this method for one year, it is expected that 5 of them will experience an accidental pregnancy.

q: Which of the following substances does not contribute to water hardness?
ex: Calcium carbonate The hardness of water is primarily caused by the presence of dissolved mineral salts of divalent cations, mainly calcium () and magnesium (). Hardness is classified into two types : temporary and permanent. Temporary hardness is caused by the presence of bicarbonate salts of calcium and magnesium, such as calcium bicarbonate () and magnesium bicarbonate (). This type of hardness can be removed by boiling the water, which causes the bicarbonates to precipitate as carbonates. Permanent hardness is caused by the presence of sulfates, chlorides, and nitrates of calcium and magnesium, such as calcium sulfate (). This type of hardness is not removed by boiling. Calcium carbonate () itself is largely insoluble in pure water and therefore does not contribute significantly to the hardness of water. It is, in fact, the precipitate (limescale) that is formed when water with temporary hardness is boiled.

q: Which of the following is not an example of direct transmission of communicable diseases?
ex: Soil The transmission of communicable diseases is broadly categorized into direct and indirect transmission. Direct transmission involves the immediate transfer of an infectious agent from an infected host or reservoir to a susceptible host. This includes : Direct contact (touching, kissing), such as in sexually transmitted diseases (STD). Droplet spread through coughing, sneezing, or talking, i.e., the respiratory route over a short distance. Transplacental or vertical transmission from mother to fetus. Indirect transmission occurs when the infectious agent is transferred via an intermediate vehicle, vector, or airborne route. Transmission through soil is a form of vehicle-borne indirect transmission. The soil acts as a reservoir for the infectious agent (e.g., tetanus spores, hookworm larvae), which can then enter a susceptible host through a break in the skin. Because the soil acts as an inanimate intermediate object, this is not considered direct transmission.

q: Acute tonsillitis most commonly involves which of the following cranial nerves?
ex: Glossopharyngeal nerve Acute tonsillitis is an infection and inflammation of the palatine tonsils, which are located in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. The primary sensory nerve supply of the tonsils is the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX). This nerve provides sensory innervation to the tonsillar region, posterior one-third of the tongue, soft palate, and oropharynx. During acute tonsillitis, inflammation stimulates the glossopharyngeal nerve endings, leading to severe throat pain. The pain may radiate to the ear because the glossopharyngeal nerve also contributes to the sensory supply of the middle ear via the tympanic branch (Jacobson’s nerve). This explains the common symptom of referred otalgia in tonsillitis. The trigeminal nerve mainly supplies the face and anterior oral cavity, the facial nerve is primarily motor to facial muscles, and the vagus nerve supplies the larynx and parts of the pharynx but is not the main sensory supply to the tonsils. Therefore, the glossopharyngeal nerve is most affected.

q: Water’s view is used to visualize which sinus for diagnostic purposes? NODIA 674===
ex: Maxillary sinus The Water's view, also known as the occipitomental view, is a specific radiographic projection used to visualize the paranasal sinuses. To obtain this view, the patient's head is tilted back so that the petrous ridges of the temporal bones are projected below the floor of the maxillary sinuses. This positioning provides an unobstructed view of the maxillary sinuses, making it the best standard radiographic view for evaluating them for fluid levels (air-fluid levels), mucosal thickening, or opacification, which are signs of sinusitis. It also provides good visualization of the floors and lateral walls of the orbits, the zygomatic bones, and the nasal septum. While other sinuses like the frontal and sphenoid sinuses are also visible on this view, the primary purpose and greatest diagnostic utility of the Water's view is the clear and unobstructed assessment of the maxillary sinuses, which are the largest of the paranasal sinuses.

q: What is the indication for a tracheostomy?
ex: Foreign body obstructing the airway A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure to create an opening into the trachea (windpipe) through the neck to establish a direct airway. The indications for tracheostomy can be broadly grouped into three categories : upper airway obstruction, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and poor pulmonary toilet (inability to clear secretions). A foreign body obstructing the airway at or above the level of the larynx that cannot be removed by other means (like the Heimlich maneuver or direct laryngoscopy) is an absolute indication for an emergent surgical airway. This bypasses the obstruction and secures a patent airway. While a cricothyroidotomy is often faster in an emergency, a tracheostomy may be performed. Tracheomalacia (C), or weakness of the tracheal cartilage, can be a complication of or an indication for tracheostomy, but obstruction is a more direct and acute reason. Vocal cord (A) and pharynx (B) replacement are not indications for this procedure.

q: Caldwell's view is used for?
ex: All of the above Caldwell’s view (occipitofrontal view) is an X-ray projection used in the assessment of the paranasal sinuses. In this view, the central beam is angled about 15° caudally, which projects the petrous ridges into the lower third of the orbits. This view clearly demonstrates the frontal sinuses, making it especially useful in diagnosing frontal sinusitis and fractures. It also provides good visualization of the anterior ethmoidal sinuses. Although the maxillary sinuses are best seen in Waters’ (occipitomental) view, they are still visible in Caldwell’s view and can be assessed to some extent. Because Caldwell’s view allows visualization of the frontal, ethmoidal, and partially the maxillary sinuses, the most appropriate answer among the given options is (D) All of the above.

q: Where will be the placement location for the Audltory Brainstem lmplant?
ex: Recess of 4th ventricle An Auditory Brainstem Implant (ABI) is used in patients who are not suitable candidates for a cochlear implant, particularly those with bilateral cochlear nerve damage, such as in neurofibromatosis type 2. Unlike a cochlear implant, which stimulates the cochlear nerve within the inner ear, an ABI directly stimulates the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem. The implant electrode array is surgically placed in the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, specifically over the cochlear nucleus on the surface of the brainstem. This location allows the device to bypass the damaged cochlea and auditory nerve and directly stimulate the central auditory pathway. The scala tympani is the placement site for a cochlear implant, not a brainstem implant. The internal auditory canal (IAC) contains cranial nerves VII and VIII but is not the site of ABI electrode placement. “Back of ear” refers to the external processor placement, not the internal electrode. Therefore, the correct placement site for an Auditory Brainstem Implant is the recess of the fourth ventricle.

q: In which condition is 100-day glaucoma observed?
ex: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) Neovascular glaucoma (NVG) is a severe, secondary form of glaucoma characterized by the growth of new, abnormal blood vessels (neovascularization) over the iris (rubeosis iridis) and into the trabecular meshwork in the anterior chamber angle. These vessels obstruct the outflow of aqueous humor, leading to a rapid and often dramatic rise in intraocular pressure. The most common cause of NVG is severe, widespread retinal ischemia. The ischemic retina releases vasoproliferative factors, primarily Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), which stimulate the neovascularization. The two main underlying conditions that cause this level of ischemia are proliferative diabetic retinopathy and ischemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO). Following an ischemic CRVO, NVG typically develops after a latent period, classically around 3 months, or approximately 100 days, earning it the historical name 100-day glaucoma.

q: Roth spots are seen in?
ex: Acute leukaemia Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages that have a white or pale center. They are a non-specific finding observed on fundoscopic examination. The white center is thought to be composed of a fibrin-platelet plug, an accumulation of inflammatory cells, or aggregates of neoplastic cells. While classically associated with subacute bacterial endocarditis, Roth spots can be seen in a wide variety of systemic conditions. These include hematological disorders such as leukemia (both acute and chronic), pernicious anemia, and thrombocytopenia. They are also seen in collagen vascular diseases like lupus, systemic infections (endocarditis, HIV), and conditions causing anoxia or vascular damage, such as diabetic retinopathy and hypertension. Therefore, among the given options, Roth spots are a well-recognized manifestation of acute leukemia, where they may represent retinal hemorrhage with a central collection of leukemic blasts. Uveal melanoma is a primary eye tumor and does not cause Roth spots.

q: Which muscle acts as the yoke muscle for the right lateral rectus?
ex: Left medial rectus Yoke muscles are pairs of extraocular muscles, one in each eye, that are the primary movers of the two eyes into a specific direction of gaze. According to Hering's law of equal innervation, when a voluntary command is sent to move the eyes, the yoke muscles in both eyes receive equal and simultaneous innervation to ensure that the movements are conjugate (coordinated). The right lateral rectus muscle is the primary abductor of the right eye, moving it to the right (dextroversion). To maintain conjugate gaze to the right, the left eye must adduct (move towards the nose). The muscle responsible for adducting the left eye is the left medial rectus. Therefore, the right lateral rectus and the left medial rectus form a yoke pair for movement of the eyes into right gaze.

q: Which organism is responsible for causing severe conjunctivitis?
ex: Neisseria Hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis is a severe, sight-threatening form of conjunctivitis characterized by a very rapid onset (within 12-24 hours) of copious purulent discharge, marked chemosis (conjunctival swelling), eyelid edema, and pain. The classic and most important cause of hyperacute conjunctivitis is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This is considered an ophthalmic emergency because the gonococcus is one of the few bacteria that can penetrate an intact corneal epithelium, leading rapidly to corneal ulceration, perforation, and permanent vision loss if not treated aggressively with systemic and topical antibiotics. Gonococcal conjunctivitis in newborns (ophthalmia neonatorum) is particularly devastating. While other bacteria like Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Haemophilus can cause acute bacterial conjunctivitis, the hyperacute and most severe form is classically associated with Neisseria.

q: Which of the following illustrates simple myopic astigmatism?
ex: -1.00 DC X 180 degree Astigmatism occurs when the eye has different refractive powers at different meridians. In simple astigmatism, one of the two principal meridians is emmetropic (in focus on the retina), while the other is either myopic or hyperopic. In Simple Myopic Astigmatism, one meridian focuses light perfectly on the retina, while the other meridian focuses light in front of the retina (myopic). The refractive correction for this would require only a cylindrical lens to correct the myopic meridian, with no spherical component needed for the emmetropic meridian. The prescription -1.00 DC X 180 degree represents a pure cylindrical correction of -1.00 diopter, which is the correct format for simple myopic astigmatism. A prescription with DS indicates a spherical correction (+1.00 DS is simple hyperopia, -1.00 DS is simple myopia). A prescription with both DS and DC (-1.00 DS-1.00 DC) represents compound myopic astigmatism.

q: Blow out fracture of orbit most commonly involves:
ex: Floor A blowout fracture is a specific type of orbital fracture that is caused by a sudden increase in intraorbital pressure from a blunt, non-penetrating trauma to the globe, such as from a fist or a ball. The force is transmitted to the orbital contents, and the pressure causes a fracture of one of the thin walls of the orbit, while the stronger orbital rim remains intact. The orbital floor (the roof of the maxillary sinus) is the most common site to be involved in a blowout fracture. The second most common site is the medial wall (the lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone). These two walls are the thinnest and weakest parts of the bony orbit. The lateral wall and the roof are much thicker and stronger and are fractured much less frequently by this mechanism. A fracture of the floor can lead to entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle, causing restricted upward gaze, and enophthalmos (sunken eye).

q: A diabetic patient develops hypopyon two days after undergoing cataract surgery. What is the appropriate management?
ex: Intravitreal antibiotics A diabetic patient developing hypopyon two days after cataract surgery is highly suggestive of acute postoperative endophthalmitis, a vision-threatening emergency. It typically presents within a few days of surgery with pain, decreased vision, redness, lid edema, and hypopyon (pus in the anterior chamber). Immediate management is critical to prevent permanent visual loss. The standard treatment is urgent intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics, commonly vancomycin (for gram-positive coverage) and ceftazidime (for gram-negative coverage), after obtaining a vitreous sample for culture and sensitivity. Topical eye drops alone (Option B) are insufficient because the infection involves the vitreous cavity. Surgery (Option C), specifically pars plana vitrectomy, may be required in severe cases or when vision is only light perception, but the first essential step is intravitreal antibiotics. No treatment (Option D) is inappropriate and dangerous. Therefore, the most appropriate immediate management is (A) Intravitreal antibiotics.

q: According to the ISNT rule, which part of the neuroretinal rim is the thinnest?
ex: Temporal The ISNT rule describes the normal configuration of the neuroretinal rim thickness in a healthy optic disc. According to this rule, the rim thickness follows the order: I > S > N > T (Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal) This means the inferior rim is the thickest, followed by the superior rim, then the nasal rim, and the temporal rim is the thinnest. The ISNT rule is clinically important in glaucoma evaluation. In glaucomatous optic neuropathy, this pattern is often disrupted, with early thinning typically occurring in the inferior and superior regions. If the rim does not follow the ISNT configuration, glaucoma should be suspected. Therefore, according to the ISNT rule, the thinnest part of the neuroretinal rim is the (C) Temporal rim.

q: Estimate the amount of Ringer’s lactate required during the first 8 hours for a 50-kg male patient with 40% second-degree burns. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon 675=== EXAMINATION PAPER 2018
ex: 4 liters Fluid resuscitation in burn patients is calculated using the Parkland formula, which is: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) burned For this patient: 4 mL × 50 kg × 40 = 8000 mL (8 litres) in the first 24 hours. According to the Parkland protocol: Half of the total fluid is given in the first 8 hours (from the time of burn injury). The remaining half is administered over the next 16 hours. So, half of 8 litres = 4 litres in the first 8 hours. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) 4 litres. Urine output (target: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour in adults) is closely monitored to adjust fluid therapy. Adequate resuscitation is essential to prevent burn shock and maintain organ perfusion.

q: In which condition is the Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) falsely elevated?
ex: Arteriosclerosis calcified arteries The Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI or ABI) is a simple, non-invasive test used to assess for peripheral artery disease (PAD). It is calculated by dividing the systolic blood pressure at the ankle by the systolic blood pressure in the arm. A normal ABI is between 1.0 and 1.4. An ABI < 0.9 is diagnostic of PAD, with the value correlating to disease severity (intermittent claudication, ischemic ulcers). However, in some patients, particularly those with long-standing diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or advanced age, the arteries of the lower leg (tibial arteries) can become heavily calcified and hardened due to medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg's sclerosis). These calcified arteries are non-compressible. When a blood pressure cuff is inflated around the ankle, it cannot fully compress the rigid artery, leading to a falsely and artificially elevated ankle pressure reading. This can result in a misleadingly normal or even abnormally high ABI (e.g., > 1.4), masking the presence of severe underlying PAD.

q: Identify the condition shown in the image.
ex: Lobar Pneumonia The image displays the gross pathological appearance of a lung affected by lobar pneumonia. This pattern of pneumonia is characterized by the inflammation and consolidation of a large, continuous area involving a significant portion or an entire lobe of a lung. The image shows the stage of red hepatization, which typically occurs in the first few days of the infection. In this stage, the affected lobe is heavy, airless, and has a consistency resembling that of a liver (hence hepatization). The reddish-brown color is due to massive congestion of the capillaries and the exudation of red blood cells, neutrophils, and fibrin into the alveolar spaces. The most common cause of classic lobar pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae. In contrast, bronchopneumonia is characterized by patchy areas of consolidation centered around bronchioles, rather than affecting an entire lobe uniformly. The other options are unrelated kidney pathologies.

q: What is the most frequent cause of chronic pancreatitis?
ex: Chronic alcohol Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterized by irreversible destruction of the pancreatic parenchyma, fibrosis, and loss of both exocrine and endocrine function. While there are numerous causes, the most common etiology by a significant margin in the Western world and many other parts of the globe is chronic and heavy alcohol consumption. Alcohol abuse is responsible for approximately 70-80% of all cases of chronic pancreatitis. Alcohol is believed to be directly toxic to pancreatic acinar cells and to alter the composition of pancreatic secretions, leading to the formation of protein plugs that obstruct small pancreatic ducts. This obstruction and direct toxicity initiate a cycle of inflammation and fibrosis that eventually destroys the gland. Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, but not chronic. Pancreatic calculi are a consequence, not a primary cause. Pancreas divisum is a congenital anomaly that is a less common cause.

q: Which of the following statements about keloid is true?
o: Extended excision is the treatment of choice
It does not extend beyond the wound
ex: It contains growth factor A keloid is a type of abnormal scar that results from an overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue, developing after a skin injury heals. Unlike a hypertrophic scar, a keloid characteristically extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound. This uncontrolled proliferation is driven by a dysregulation in the wound healing process, involving an overproduction of extracellular matrix components, particularly collagen. A key factor in this pathogenesis is the excessive production of various growth factors, most notably Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) and Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF). These growth factors stimulate fibroblasts to proliferate and synthesize collagen at an abnormally high rate, leading to the formation of the large, raised scar tissue. Statement (C) is incorrect, as extending beyond the wound margin is the defining feature of a keloid. Simple wide excision (B) is not the treatment of choice as it is associated with an extremely high recurrence rate, often resulting in an even larger keloid. Treatment is challenging and usually involves a combination of therapies like intralesional steroid injections, cryotherapy, or excision with adjuvant radiation.

q: Which nerve is thickened in the image shown?
ex: Greater auricular nerve The image shows marked thickening of a nerve in the head and neck region, a classic sign of leprosy (Hansen's disease). The nerve shown is the greater auricular nerve. This is a sensory nerve that arises from the cervical plexus (C2, C3) and ascends vertically over the sternocleidomastoid muscle towards the ear. It supplies sensation to the skin over the angle of the jaw, the parotid gland, and a large part of the auricle (ear). The greater auricular nerve is one of the most commonly affected peripheral nerves in leprosy, along with the ulnar and common peroneal nerves. Its superficial course makes it easily visible and palpable when it becomes thickened due to the inflammatory and granulomatous infiltration caused by Mycobacterium leprae. Thickening of this nerve, often associated with loss of sensation in its distribution, is a cardinal sign of leprosy.

q: Which tissue layers are incised during a fasciotomy?
o: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia
ex: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia A fasciotomy is an emergency surgical procedure performed to treat acute compartment syndrome. Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a confined fascial compartment compromises the circulation and function of the tissues within that space, potentially leading to muscle and nerve necrosis. The goal of the procedure is to relieve this pressure by decompressing the affected compartment(s). To achieve this, the surgeon must make an incision through all the layers that are confining the swollen muscle. This involves making a long incision through the skin, followed by the underlying subcutaneous tissue and the superficial fascia. The most critical step is then to incise the tough, inelastic deep fascia that encases the muscle compartment. This final incision allows the swollen muscle to bulge out, immediately relieving the intra compartmental pressure and restoring blood flow. Merely incising the skin and subcutaneous layers would be insufficient to decompress the muscle compartment, which is the primary goal of the procedure.

q: Which of the following statements about Crohn’s disease is not true?
ex: Continuous lesion visualized in endoscopy Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. One of its hallmark features is the discontinuous nature of the inflammation, which is described as skip lesions. This means there are areas of active inflammation separated by segments of normal-appearing mucosa. Therefore, the statement that a continuous lesion is visualized on endoscopy is not true and is, in fact, the characteristic pattern of ulcerative colitis, where inflammation typically starts in the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous and circumferential manner. In Crohn's disease, the rectum is often spared (A). Histological examination frequently reveals non-caseating granulomas (C), another hallmark of the disease. The combination of deep linear ulcers and transmural inflammation with submucosal edema creates a nodular appearance of the mucosa on endoscopy or barium studies, which is described as a cobblestone appearance (D).

q: What is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing carcinoma of the pancreatic head?
ex: EUS (Endoscopic Ultrasound) For the diagnosis and staging of pancreatic cancer, particularly tumors in the head of the pancreas, Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) is considered the most sensitive and accurate imaging modality. EUS involves passing an endoscope with a high-frequency ultrasound transducer at its tip into the stomach and duodenum. This allows for high-resolution imaging of the pancreas from a very close proximity, without interference from bowel gas. EUS is superior to CT and MRI for detecting small tumors (<2 cm), assessing the depth of tumor invasion, and evaluating local lymph node involvement and vascular invasion (T and N staging). A crucial advantage of EUS is that it also allows for EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA), which can be performed during the same procedure to obtain a tissue diagnosis. This combination of superior imaging and the ability to obtain a cytological sample makes EUS the best single investigation for both diagnosing and staging pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. ERCP is more therapeutic for relieving biliary obstruction.
